items.body:
Bang Chan is heading to Singapore for Grand Prix week.

The Stray Kids leader will make an appearance at the Breitling x Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Pop-Up at Raffles City on 10 October at 11AM. During his visit, he will explore the activation before stopping by the Breitling Raffles City Boutique.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

Running from 3 to 12 October, the pop-up celebrates the Swiss watchmaker’s partnership with the Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Team, bringing watchmaking and motorsport together during Singapore Grand Prix week.

Fans can also test their timing with the “B” Challenge by Breitling, a digital game that gives participants 60 seconds to stop a moving chronograph at the 12 o’clock mark. Prizes include a Breitling Navitimer B01 Chronograph 43, exclusive Breitling x Aston Martin Aramco Formula One merchandise, and Breitling merchandise.

The pop-up is open daily from 10AM to 10PM at Raffles City Shopping Centre, 252 North Bridge Road, #01-35.

items.excerpt: Juri Seo thrives in the balance of complex compositional processes and aesthetic bliss. items.body: Black album covers are fairly rare; Prince’s The Black Album comes to mind, along with Thembi Soddell’s black-on-black Love Songs, which includes a book of black print on black pages. Rachel Shearer is the latest addition to this small group, as Te Oro a te Ao (the resounding of the world) presents black type on a black background. The hue honors Hinenuitepō, the goddess of night and death, and issues a warning on climate change. Shearer reflects her Aotearoan (New Zealand) roots by translating the Māori concept of whakapapa into aural form. The belief that all of nature, including time, is connected forms the basis of this work. The opening “Waha” (featuring Cathy Livermore) means both gate and voice, and serves as an entry point not only to the album, but to the spiritual world. It arrives as an invocation or incantation, at first a cappella, then layered, then sanded with dirt, dust and rock. Over time it becomes a choir, its sedimentary layers accumulating until they solidify into a drone. Is this the earth speaking, or our ancestors, or the buzz of time? The collective sound overtakes the individual without sublimating her power. The heart of the album is the two-part “Pounamu Becoming Crystal.” The first part reflects the “movement and strength of water,” which begins as a mist yet transforms into a torrent. While experiencing such dynamic contrast, one may think of everything from the act of creation to the destruction of the planet. The piece incorporates “subterranean volcanic activity, tectonic plate movements and land slippages,” and acts as a parable of disruption. Yet by the end, the timbres soften, offering a modicum of hope; perhaps time’s arrow is instead a cycle. The second segment, subtitled “Wiriwiri” (to tremble), honors the dance of Tānerore: the visible shimmer of hot air as it rises from the ground. At first, the piece continues the rumbling timbres of its predecessor, but these give way to white noise: the processed sound of cicadas, whose volume increases with the temperature. As Earth warms, the cries of the cicadas grow ever more insistent. “Ao” is a flexible word that can mean “sunrise,” “clouds” or even “world.” This gentle guitar coda suggests a manner of living on the planet, honoring sound with sound, presence with presence, gift with gift. While this is the Māori way, it is not often replicated, especially in Western societies. The arc of the album – invitation, experience, farewell – suggests a mode of interaction that posits all creation, animate and inanimate, as partners, the breath of heat mingling with the breath of life, the audible with the inaudible, the present with the absent and the yet-to-come. (Richard Allen)

items.body: In “Rokia”, a young villager falls in love with his neighbour, and her mother, Rokia, opposes the relationship. Rabie Houti, a violinist and singer from Oran in Algeria who has lived in Montpellier since 2014, tells the story with Gasba Électrique, who combine Maghrebi flute with electronic textures. The track brings together his Arabo-Andalusian violin, electronic beats and rock guitars, and builds gradually into a trance. Trance is the band’s own word for its live shows too, which have taken them from Montpellier to Canada, Algeria and Kazakhstan. Houti’s own road to those stages started in Oran, where his father loved Arabo-Andalusian music and his older sister Khedija taught him his first notes on a mandolin. Around the age of eight he played his first concert, on violin, with the junior orchestra of the Nassim El Andalous school at Oran’s opera house. These days he leads the Rabie Houti Band, active since 2017, who set Maghrebi melodies over funk and rock grooves and place themselves in “Sono Mondiale”, the movement the late Rachid Taha championed. Joudour, their second album, takes its title from the Arabic word for roots, and the band marked its release with a free show at Rockstore in Montpellier on 3 October. It follows Tahtaha from 2019, which Houti describes as a test from a time when the band was still searching; with Joudour, he says, they found their signature. The new album leans further into rock and electronics, and every track is an original composition. You can stream “Rokia” and Joudour HERE. The post Daily Discovery: Rabie Houti – Rokia appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Her grandmother had run out of stories for the night. Go to the cow pen, she told six-year-old Kasiva Mutua , and listen to the secret the black bull is telling the white one. Kasiva went, listened, and returned having heard nothing but a bull sniffing the air. Her grandmother sent her back, told her to listen properly, that the secret was being told right now. The second time, she heard it. Crickets layered on top of each other. Cows breathing in something close to a shared tempo. Wind moving through the trees, laughter drifting from the kitchen. She started humming what she’d heard, then playing it out on her own bed frame, her lap, her chest and cheeks, and from there on anything within reach: pans, spoons, a school desk, a bucket. Percussion belonged to men in the community she grew up in. She took it up anyway, and kept at it until she was one of the only women in Kenya playing it at all, continentally or internationally, and eventually one of the best known. By 25 years old, she was a OneBeat Fellow, and the following year she joined The Nile Project, an East African touring collective she’s stayed with since. Two years later, in 2015, she co-founded MOTRAMUSIC in Nairobi, Kenya’s first all-female percussion collective, taking young women through a year of mentorship in rhythm, composition and performance. She’s also worked with Giant Steps Music and recorded for Coke Studio Africa. TED named her a Global Fellow in 2017, and she has spoken about the drum as a way of telling her own story. In 2020 a OneBeat Accelerator grant let her build Vibe na Queen, an online platform connecting Kenyan women musicians through the pandemic. Her 2022 debut EP Ngewa came after all of that, carrying what the teaching and the touring had put into her playing, and Desturi, her debut album released in February last year, picked up where it left off. Fifteen years, Kasiva says, is how long she has wanted to play WOMEX, hearing it talked about long before she ever stood near its stage, called the World Cup of performances by everyone who had been. On 23 October, in Las Palmas, it happens. She is bringing the album with her, and an open invitation: find her showcase, and come share it. She answered our questions for this year’s Musical Road to WOMEX, on the drum as a way of telling stories, on growing up in a place where it wasn’t meant to be hers, and on what she wants to find on the islands, and put together a playlist exclusively for Rhythm Passport, the tracks hers to choose.  You’ve described the drum as a way of telling your people’s stories. For someone hearing you for the first time, how would you introduce the sound you make now, and where does the voice sit alongside the percussion? Rhythm is a universal language. It’s also everywhere around us. It’s heard, felt, it brings movement (dance, nod, make faces of expression) and evokes emotions. There’s no one who is excluded from rhythm. Children, adults, animals, people of different abilities and backgrounds; we all understand and experience it. We carry rhythm within us throughout our lives, and when the rhythm stops, life ends. For someone hearing me for the first time, I’m a gentle reminder of the joy of having rhythm and how important it is to notice it. The way rhythm sounds and is expressed can vary depending on where we come from, our travels, experiences, and the people and environments we encounter. But in all those variations, is the same foundation; rhythm is something we all carry within us. My sound, then, is something familiar, rooted in East Africa and shaped by nature, my experiences, stories, and the many influences of our African cultures. You learned drumming from your grandmother in a community where the instrument was reserved for men. Looking back, what was the moment you understood that playing it would define your life rather than simply defy a rule? I was inspired by my grandmother’s stories that she told me that taught me to listen to nature. And that way, I started hearing sounds and eventually rhythm. I don’t think there’s an exact moment that stood out, rather a consistent chain of events that led me here. But I can remember a moment I asked myself “Surely, what else in the world can bring me this kind of joy? I LOVE this thing!” WOMEX lands this year in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, an Atlantic island with its own percussion: the tajaraste, driven by drum and chácaras, the big castanets thought to trace back to the islands’ North African roots. As a percussionist, what are you most curious to hear there? Eeeeeeeverything, man! I wanna hear everything! From the music, to how the children there laugh, and how the water hits the rocks. I’m very curious about the island’s stories too! In a WOMEX line-up full of the world’s traditions, what makes your showcase stand out, and what do you most want people to take from it? My best friend says that there’s nothing as beautiful as watching someone fully immersed in something they absolutely love. There’s something about witnessing that kind of joy; it makes you fall in love with them, and somehow, in the process, you fall in love with yourself all over again. Well… WOMEX is built on unexpected meetings. Are there particular artists, labels or collaborators you’re hoping to cross paths with in Las Palmas? Yes, I’m looking forward to the beautiful connections that will be born out of WOMEX. I’m particularly excited to meet female artists and instrumentalists, some who I have already connected on Instagram, and women working across the music industry. Your drumming is built to pull people in: call and response, bodies moving. A WOMEX audience is mostly music professionals, there to watch and assess rather than dance. How do you win a room like that? Yes, they may be music professionals, but before anything else, they’re human. They are someone’s son, somebody’s daughter. They have kids, They have feelings, emotions, relationships, memories, pain and joy. They’re an audience like any other. Rhythm doesn’t choose where to land or who it belongs to. Even I, myself, cannot control that. It simply does what it does. My role is to play and let it find its way to whoever is listening. Your travels have a way of turning up in your music. Ahead of your first time in the Canaries, is there anything about the islands, their rhythms, their sounds, you’re hoping to come away with? My travels have constantly shaped the person I am becoming. My interactions, experiences and stories all play a big part in the music to come. I’m very curious what this part of my musical journey will look like. In much of Africa the drum has been a man’s instrument, off-limits to women, and you are one of the few who took it up, made a life of it, and spent years bringing other women in behind you. Is there a message you feel especially compelled to carry to an international audience through this showcase? Ah yes. The beauty of our African cultures is that they are deeply complex and constantly evolving. I’ve lived through a time, before mobile phones and the internet, and now I’m living through this period of cultural transition, where we’re all negotiating what we carry forward and how it interacts with the world now. For a long time, the focus was on me being a woman holding a drum. But I think the focus needs to shift from who is playing the instrument to what is being played. I’ve dedicated my life to making sure the rhythms of my people continue to live and travel beyond home, to places where strangers can hear them, dance to them, and perhaps find something of themselves in them. It used to feel significant to be the only woman in the room holding a drum. Today, I’m less interested in that distinction. I’m more interested in the joy of sharing the music, traditions and stories that live within those rhythms, and allowing that to take centre stage. Having moved from percussion into songwriting, production and your own voice, what’s next? New recordings, new collaborations, a direction you haven’t tried yet? I’d prefer to see it as an “expansion of rhythm”. As I evolve, I am finding new ways of expression. I am very open to cultural evolution, and this brings in the aspect of collaboration. Traveling has deeply shaped who I’m becoming and interacting with different cultures adds to my musical DNA. Yes, there’s lots of music to come. Yes, there’s collaborations and yes, there’s many directions I haven’t tried and perhaps are unknown to me just yet. I’m also excited to discover this! If you could write a personal invitation to the people arriving in Las Palmas to come and find your showcase, what would it say? Let me tell you a little story… For about 15 years, as I backed many artists in Kenya and around the world, I always heard this name “WOMEX”. And how it was said to me meant “This is the ‘World Cup’ of performances!” I always wanted to play here. With anyone really. I just wanted to get on this stage. More than 15 years later, it’s going to happen! And with my Desturi, my debut album. WOMEX don’t really understand what they’ve done! They’ve allowed me to live a dream, and by doing so, have now given me permission to take on other dreams… My name is Kasiva Mutua. Find my showcase and come, share my dream come true with me on 23rd Oct, massive Friday night! I’d love to have you there! The bigger the party, the bigger the celebration! Yay! Ahsante! I love you!   Fifteen years of hearing WOMEX talked about end on a Friday night at Plaza del Espigón in Las Palmas. Kasiva Mutua plays there on 23 October, and she's already told the city what she wants from it: the bigger the party, the bigger the celebration!   PLAYLIST: KASIVA MUTUA X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Kasiva Mutua appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by UMUR — "Section X" is the second full-length studio album by Danish power/progressive metal act BeyondTwilight (if you discount the two Twilight albums as the works of another band). The album wasreleased through Massacre Records in March 2005. It�s the successor to "The Devil's Hall of Fame"from 2001. The nucleus of the band is intact (namely keyboard player and band founder Finn Zierler,guitarist Anders Ericson Kragh, bassist Anders Lindgren, and drummer Tomas Fred�n) since the releaseof "The Devil's Hall of Fame" but there have been a couple of lineup changes. The omnipresent JacobHansen (Invocator, Anubis Gate, Pyramaze...etc.) has joined on guitars and vocals, and American leadvocalist Kelly Sundown Carpenter (Darkology, Inner Sanctum, Outworld...etc.) has replaced Norwegianvocalist J�rn Lande (Ark, Masterplan, Allen - Lande...etc.).Stylistically the material on "Section X" is a combination of epic power metal and heavy metaloriented progressive metal. The latter means that this is progressive oriented music but nottechnical for the sake of it, and you shouldn't expect long instrumental sections dominating thetracks. Beyond Twilight�s music is more song oriented and generally features relatively accessibleverse/chorus structures. The tracks are quite sophisticated though (listen to the almost theatrical"Sleeping Beauty"). The closest relative is to my ears Symphony X because of the power metal andprogressive metal hybrid style, but also because of the epic nature of the music, the heaviness ofthe music (this is not vanilla Euro power metal), and the omnipresence of keyboards. Carpenter isquite the impressive singer with a strong voice and commanding delivery and the musicianship isgenerally through the roof on this release."Section X" features a powerful, heavy, and detailed sound production. It�s polished and wellproduced but still heavy and raw enough not to become too sterile sounding. Every instrument andvocal part stand out in the mix and are perfectly balanced. Just because this is Zierler�s projectdoesn�t mean that the keyboards overshadow everything else. On the contrary Zierler is veryconscious in terms of when his keyboards should dominate a track and when they shouldn�t. Uponconclusion "Section X" is a step up in quality from the already great "The Devil's Hall of Fame" andit�s just through and through a high quality release from Beyond Twilight. A 4 - 4.5 star (85%)rating is deserved.(Originally posted on Metal Music Archives).

After all, what's the pointof music if it doesn't entertain you and put a smile on your face?This album will never be mentioned in the same breath as the undisputed giants of progressive rock,but that hardly matters. It's a record I keep coming back to, and one I enjoy tremendously. Germanoddballs Nine Days Wonder, a band that seemed determined to reinvent themselves with every release,followed up their wonderfully bizarre debut by making a complete stylistic U-turn. The result is analbum that's surprisingly difficult to pin down.If I had to try, I'd place it somewhere between David Bowie and Van der Graaf Generator, with atouch of Genesis and Nektar sprinkled on top. What they play could broadly be called progressiverock, but that's only part of the story. There's glam rock swagger, flashes of krautrock, bursts ofhard rock, hints of jazz rock, and all of it fronted by a wonderfully (!) theatrical vocalist. Inother words, this album stubbornly refuses to sit in a single genre box.The band's greatest strength is its energy. Driven by swirling organs and keyboards, backed by aheavy and aggressive bass, they charge through inventive progressive rock that somehow manages tocombine the punch of hard rock with the structure of prog and the occasional hook of melodic pop-rock. Had I not known they were German, I would have guessed they were British without hesitation.Side A is a thoroughly enjoyable affair, filled with melodic songs that contain just enoughprogressive trickery to keep things interesting. But it's on Side B that the real fun begins. Herethe band completely lets loose, delivering colorful, adventurous prog rock with the magnificentnine-minute epic "We Grasp the Naked Meat" as the undisputed centerpiece.We Never Lost Control is a lovable little gem of an album: quirky, energetic, unpretentious, andendlessly entertaining. Think of it as a bag of mixed candy for progressive rock fans. Maybe itisn't a masterpiece, but it's the sort of record that reminds you why digging through the lesser-known corners of the genre can be so rewarding.

items.body: Review by yarstruly — This is from my blog "Scott's Song by Song Spotlights" with links for listening and purchasing.Clicked 5, but really a 4.5...4 is too low!T.A.P are a progressive rock band led by composer/keyboardist Michael Jobborn. On their first album, which I have not heard (2023's "Paradigms") the band was rounded out by Warr-guitarist/multi-instrumentalist Mark Cook (Phase of Twilight and others) and Guitarist/Vocalist/multi-instrumentalist Suzi James (Fearful Symmetry, whose wonderful latest album "I've Started?So I'll Finish" is reviewed on this blog as well!). Paul Sears and Bill Bachman were both contributors on the first album on the drum throne. This time around Bill Bachman is a full member. Bill is renowned for his work as a drumming educator, including his work with several Drum Corps around the US. (DCI- Drum Corps International- is a deep rabbit hole that I have been familiar with since my college days!) But his prog resume is impressive as well: (From the press release) "Bill is the drummer for Herd of Instinct, Spoke of Shadows, has toured with progressive rock artist Neal Morse, is on recordings with Trey Gunn (King Crimson), Colin Edwin (Porcupine Tree), Adam Holzman (Miles Davis & Steven Wilson), and Gerald Albright (Grammy award winning saxophonist)". So, the musical talent in this band is absolutely staggering!This album comes courtesy of Anne-Claire Rallo of Bad Dog Promotions. As always, I receive no additional compensation and am free to "call it like I hear it". In fact, when I received the email offering this review to me from Anne-Claire, I replied, "You had me at Suzi James". The album "Paradigms II" is to be released on October 3, 2026, on the Prog Rock Essentials label (Ordering info follows the review). As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Time to dig into the music!T.A.P are:Michael Jobborn - concepts, keysMark Cook - Warr guitar, bass, 12-string guitar, synth, sitar, strings, choirSuzi James - acoustic/electric guitars, keys, flute, violinBill Bachman - drums, percussionAdditional Contributors on tracks:2. Chris Gill - guitarChris Messina - synth4. Steve Bonino - guitar, lyrics/vocals5. Gayle Ellett - mellotron, acoustic/electric guitars6. Massimo Pieretti - piano, synthGayle Ellett - bouzouki, mellotron8. Tenk van Dool - mandolin, guitarChris Gill - guitarTrack 1 - Galaxy Unknown (4:28)An organ riff, accented with drums starts us off with an odd meter. The rest of the band soon joins in. There is a guitar solo after around 45 seconds. A softer section follows with alternating acoustic and electric instruments in the spotlight. This is a wonderful instrumental musical journey with many layers. As one might expect, the talent level here is through the roof! A terrific opener!Track 2 - A Beacon of Light (12:17)This one fades in with some guitar effects and synth tones. It feels like the first rays of sunlight at dawn, matching the title. Electric piano chords bring a sense of rhythm. The bass line provides melodic movement. The chords are layered among many instruments, giving a rich tonal palate. This is moving at a moderately slow tempo and a relaxed feel. The guitar solo that happens at around the 4-minute mark brings a balance of melodicism and complexity. A droning section after that leads to an upbeat groove on the bass and drums. It begins to take on a jazz fusion flavor. Synth and guitar solos float over the top of the rhythm bed. Just before 7:30 things calm down and a new section begins. Sitar sounds are a part of the soundscape. Bill's marching band experience shows in his snare part. At 8:45 we are down to lead guitar, bass and keys. The drums subtly return. We are in a slower 6-8 at this point. At 9:55 a more strident beat that reminds me of old TV themes takes over. There are so many moods in this piece; I love it! At 11:30, it reminds me of how it began. What an absolutely fantastic instrumental piece of music!Track 3 - A Dramatic Interlude (4:06)Electric piano, bass and lead guitar start this off. The drums enter a moment later. This is in a moderately slow 6-8, so far, but the title tells me something is going to happen. The tempo increases slightly and becomes more rhythmic after a small crescendo. I believe that is the Warr guitar taking the solo that follows. I love the staccato bass and guitar riff at around 2:20. Things begin to build up at around 3:20. The track ends with a long, sustained chord. A wonderful piece, but not as dramatic as the title indicated. Track 4 - A Hole in the Ground (6:14)Rich electric piano chords and clean guitars start us off here. Lead guitar emerges. And then--Vocals! Guest musician Steve Bonino is on this track with guitars and vocals. (This is not the first time his name has appeared in one of my reviews!) The drums begin to emerge as we progress. Mark Cook's basslines are fantastic on this album. Steve's voice seems a little buried in the mix at times. The drums might be a little too far back at times, as well. I like the song, but I don't feel like it's mixed as well as it could be. It would benefit from a better presentation. It ends with droning sounds.Track 5 - 4th Dimensional Wave (11:50)Sound effects fade in and guitars join. This starts out sounding like some sort of alarm. Soon, though, the music gets melodic with a fantastic guitar solo; I believe it is Suzi James. We are in a moderately slow tempo. The keys are playing a mellotron style chorus behind the solo. Some intricate rhythmic patterns follow. This keeps building, slowly and gradually. At around 4:20 we get into odd meters. At 5:45, the rhythm shifts into a different groove. I am really enjoying this one! There are tons of changes! Gayle Ellet of Djam Karet and his band the Electromags adds his keyboard abilities to the soundscapes. Probably my favorite track, so far.Track 6 - Lyrical Paradox (3:50)This one has a bit of a swing to it. Sort of a mellow melodic tune. The sound gets bigger just after the one-minute mark. Great melodies in this one. I love the slide guitar in it; it reminds me of the slide guitar in "And You and I" from Yes. This is a nice little piece. Ellet is back with bouzouki on this, and Massimo Pieretti (whom I have reviewed as well) adds keyboards.Track 7 - Outlooks of the Closed-Minded (6:29)This opens with some accents and jazz chords. It has a fusion feel to my ears. I love the syncopated rhythms. It reminds me of the Dixie Dregs a bit. Lots of melodies wind their way through this one. Wonderful track!Track 8 - Wishful Solitude (:)This one is more up-tempo, yet lighthearted. As with most of the album, the melodies are abundant! At around 3:15 Suzi plays her flute. There are many interesting things in the soundscape. At just be for the 5-minute mark, a descending synth part that sounds like the 70s idea of a UFO landing takes over, then we get a bit funky! At around 6:45 we get a psychedelic organ sound. This is a very cool piece with many different things going on. Tenk van Dool (who I am not familiar with) plays the mandolin at around 8:45. The melodies intertwine as we approach the ending. This is a wonderfully arranged prog instrumental. Great way to end this wonderful album.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:I really liked that a lot! Unfortunately, I am not sure what happened on track 4, "A Hole in the Ground". I have always liked Steve Bonino's contributions, and he always seems to be a good guy in the online interactions I have had with him, but something just didn't work for me on that track. Otherwise, this is a fantastic album of mainly instrumental prog with some fusion tendencies. I give this a 4.5 out of 5 or 90%. Recommended!

items.body: Review by Aussie-Byrd-Brother — Not all prog-related albums need to hold overly complex arrangements, a new case in point being 2026's `Trauma', the sixth disc from frequent Yes/Asia keyboardist Geoff Downes DBA (Downes Braide Association) project that sees him teaming up with pop/rock vocalist, song-writer and producer Chris Braide. The latter's work (check out the eclectic smorgasbord of pop artists the guy has worked for!) results in a series of highly melodic, catchy and sophisticated pop/rock/AOR tunes here all given light prog-rock embellishments, the duo backed up by frequent DBA contributor, bassist Andy Hodge, drummers Ashley Soan (Rick Wakeman) and Tim Weller (The Oscillation), and multi-instrumentalist Dave Bainbridge (Iona).In Chris Braide's own words, the album is described as being "about the ghosts we inherit, the wounds we hide, and the light that still finds its way through. In the end, it is not an album about suffering, but survival. 'Trauma' isn't an album about defeat - it's about what happens after. It's about carrying your scars with dignity, refusing to be diminished, and remembering that kindness and perseverance ultimately outlast cruelty and fear." Despite the recurring theme, lower that raised eye-brow, prog fan, and step away from the Roger Dean cover, this ain't no concept album! But many of the tunes take a similar approach, displaying fancy pop-smarts with rousing choruses, soaring harmonies and crisp instrumental touches. A softer and less bombastic Asia might be a gentle comparison, although the tunes are more reflective, even if they both share a `radio friendly' approach (if popular radio was actually taking a chance on songs like this these days!).Looking at some of the highlights, after an Asia-esque fanfare, poppy opener `Hello, Hello' unveils a catchy recurring chorus and gliding harmonies, Chris Braide's voice revealing a charismatic rasp. The title track, one of the longer pieces at over eight minutes, is certainly one of more dramatic moments with its reassuring words, dreamy guitar strains and thoughtful piano dancing around shifting tempo changes, and is bound to be considered an album standout.The sweet and upbeat `Wonderland' slinks with programmed beats, jangling guitars, purring synths and a buoyant chorus that wouldn't be unexpected from any of the country rockers that are currently very popular. While not quite a duet, `Love and Loss' has Chris complimented vocally by British-Australian singer-songwriter Emmi (Emily Joy Green) - think Sound of Contact's `Beyond Illumination' or `Time Stands Still' from Rush for a similar effect. The ear-worm chorus of `I Wish I'd Known' is dream-pop perfection, `Do You Remember?' could be an Eighties pop-era Genesis out-take (sounds like it could have easily ended up on `Duke' or `Abacab'), and Chris comes together with synth-pop icon Marc Almond on pressing lament `Juliet'.Most prog-fans will gravitate towards the longest track here at nearly fifteen minutes the most, and `Lake of Memories' is a slowly unfolding multi-part suite with recurring passages across a solid mix of gentle reflective moments and driving rock passages. Each reprise of the enlivening chorus grows in urgency and power, and the constantly elegant synth-orchestration, Andy Hodge's sweetly murmuring bass and weeping guitar soloing throughout reminds of UK proggers Pendragon at their romantic best. It pairs nicely with the thoughtful and moving closer `Wherever You are Now', an emotive paean to a former love with a triumphant end.`Trauma' is perhaps a little long at nearly an hour, some listeners may find the polished-to-perfection production to be impossibly clean and the progressive elements too subdued, but there's no denying there's an exemplary range of quality song-writing, warming vocals and tasteful playing from Downes, Braide and company on display here. Give it a few spins, and listen for how this gem reveals its strengths.Four stars - but if you're a stuffy prog-snob who can't accept anything even a little poppy, just take a half-point off and walk away! ;)

items.body: Review by Andis — Or, as it should probably have been called: The Endless Intro.Nobody needs to tell me this album is built from leftovers from previous sessions. After listeningto it, that fact practically introduces itself. In theory, recycling old material could have been agreat idea if anyone involved had possessed the energy, inspiration, or curiosity to actually dosomething interesting with it. Instead, the apparent creative process was: find some unused RichardWright keyboard recordings, sprinkle on a bit of guitar, drums, and the occasional mysteriousspaceship noise, then glue everything together and call it an album. Any questions?What makes this even more frustrating is that Pink Floyd is one of my favorite bands of all time.I've spent decades loving their music, so this isn't coming from a casual listener looking forsomething to complain about. If anything, I wanted to love this album more than anyone.Unfortunately, enthusiasm can only carry you so far when the music seems determined to driftaimlessly into the horizon.This record taught me an important life lesson: always listen before you buy. When I heard PinkFloyd were releasing a new album, I was so excited that I pre-ordered it immediately. That was amistake of truly Floydian proportions. I haven't been this bored since listening to The Final Cut.On the bright side, this album didn't make me quite as depressed, so I suppose that's progress.The Endless River is quite literally The Endless Intro. It feels like an introduction that somehowescaped containment and continued for over 52 minutes. If we're being generous, we can count thefinal track as an actual song, which brings the intro down to a mere 46 minutes. Was that song worthsitting through a 46-minute introduction? No. No, it was not.When you put the Pink Floyd name on an album, people naturally expect something resembling PinkFloyd. Not a 52-minute ambient soundscape that vaguely gestures toward Pink Floyd while offeringabsolutely nothing we haven't heard before, and usually heard done better. This is less a new albumand more a museum tour of discarded ideas.I'm giving it two stars, and that's me being charitable. There are a few pleasant moments scatteredthroughout the record, but they're buried beneath such a thick layer of mediocrity that excavatingthem feels like a part-time job.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are times when reality is stranger than fiction, and the story behind the making of this album is another example of that. Philippe DeBarge was a young French heir to a pharmaceutical fortune and a huge fan of The Pretty Things. Guitarist Dick Taylor had become disillusioned by the lack of impact of S.F. Sorrow, leading Victor Unitt to join the band as his replacement; this was the first album he recorded with them. DeBarge contacted the musicians and invited them to his opulent ch�teau in Saint-Tropez to propose a deal: he would fund their stay and record an album with himself as the lead vocalist. There, at the Epi-Plage club and his own residence, a thoroughly bohemian gathering took place, reminiscent of a Fran�oise Sagan novel; French rock legend Johnny Hallyday and actress Brigitte Bardot mingled and played guitar amidst a black-and-white "Nouvelle Vague" atmosphere. The album was recorded in London at Nova Studios. Thanks to DeBarge's funding, The Pretty Things had access to high-quality equipment, including an 8-track tape recorder.After the recording sessions, DeBarge took the masters to France, and the material remained in storage, unreleased and forgotten, on acetate discs. The acetate has been bootlegged since then. In 2010, it was acquired by Mike Stax, owner of the 1960s music magazine Ugly Things. He unearthed one of the two acetates, had it mixed and mastered, and then, as a bonus track, It led the classic Pretty Things lineup, which Dick Taylor had just left at the time the tracks with DeBarge were recorded, to record a song titled "Monsieur Rock" (Philippe's Ballad) as a bonus track for this release on Ugly Things UTCD-2207.The songs "Alexander," "Eagle's Son," and "It'll Never Be Me" were already known, having been recorded in the late 1960s by "Electric Banana", the pseudonym under which The Pretty Things recorded soundtracks for De Wolfe Music. Notably, these three songs appear in Menahem Golan's film What's Good for the Goose (1969).The Philippe DeBarge album itself serves as a bridge between the group's major Works, S.F. Sorrow and Parachute, yet it stands on its own merits. Less dark than its predecessor, it is perhaps the final example of that fresh, unpredictable, exciting, and thrilling, yet fun, psychedelia. This is evident in the opening track, "Hello, How Do You Do," which echoes the trippier side of the Rolling Stones' Their Satanic Majesties era, while the restrained calm of "You Might Even Say" recalls the Kinks. The track "Alexandre" is vocally challenging, raw and pugnacious, reminiscent of the early Who, yet it takes flight thanks to the Pretty Things' backing vocals and Victor Unitt's diverse guitar solos; these solos explore various shades of psychedelia while occasionally channeling the wild spirit of his previous group, the Edgar Broughton Band.These tracks sit alongside others with a more pop-oriented sound, charming thanks to the use of the clavichord, as in "Send You With Loving," and a prominent bassline. The album's real strength lies in its garage-rock, almost proto-punk, tracks, which are packed with energy and vocal harmonies, blending acoustic Indian ethnic elements with rock 'n' roll piano, as heard in "You're Running You And Me." "Peace" possesses a unique poetry and beauty, and is linked to "Eagle's Son," carrying forward its infectious rhythm and energy. It features melodies full of personality, where the rock and pop of "Swinging London" float through, almost becoming anthems of the era.While the influence of the Beatles could be traced in FS Sorrow, here we find psychedelia driven by acoustic guitar and harpsichord, punctuated by bursts of distorted electric guitar in soundscapes closer to the Kinks. The work evokes an era when the past and the future did not clash, simply because they were distinct, as seen in "New Day." Wally Waller handles piano and organ duties on "It'll Never Be Me", a track that remains laid-back right up until Victor Unitt's screeching solo, while the bongo percussion adds a relaxing touch that contrasts with the album's more urgent moments."Monsieur Rock (Ballad Of Philippe)" sounds more modern yet fits the spirit perfectly; it is even moving, evoking an era where the backing vocals and guitar seem to pick up exactly where they left off. The sound is raw, defiant, and powerful, with an improvisational feel, making it a fitting tribute that brings a sense of currency and relevance to this long-awaited official release.Twink left in late 1969 to form Pink Fairies. Skip Alan returned on drums just in time for the band's return to Abbey Road to begin work on Parachute, which retained the psychedelic sound but incorporated increasingly progressive elements. And Philippe DeBarge shines like those teenage memories that, as time goes by, leave you wondering if they were real or imagined...distorted like that very psychedelia, a time capsule that endures like the eternally fair weather of the Saint-Tropez coast.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Few late-80s metal albums are as influential as Savatage's fourth studio offering 'Hall of theMountain King', originally released by Atlantic. This is the first album by the American bandproduced by then-new producer Paul O'Neill, who had insisted on a more coherent musical direction,while also adding a bit of a conceptual edge to their recordings. At the same time, the band shows awillingness to experiment with more sophisticated arrangements and tighter compositions, as heardthroughout the album. The result is a darker, progressive-oriented record that sits at theintersection of melodic power metal and technical heavy metal, offering a triumphant and relentlesssound graced by fast-paced guitars and stunning vocal performances. As usual, fantastical elementsprevail on this Savatage album, bringing along an interesting aesthetic that sets the band apartfrom many of its contemporaries in the heavy metal scene. The lack of success of their previousalbums may have motivated Savatage to create a solid, kind of "bulletproof" collection of songs,that is what the record feels like.The straightforward songwriting, thunderous solos, and the overall dark atmosphere of 'Hall of theMountain King' render this album an appealing listen from start to finish. Its ten tracks areprimarily written by Jon and Criss Oliva, respectively lead singer and lead guitarist of the band,while a few songs also credit producer O'Neill as a co-writer. This record also has instrumentalarrangements of excerpts from 'In the Hall of the Mountain King' by Grieg and 'Mars, the Bringer ofWar' by Holst, which is further proof that Savatage were pursuing a sophistication of their soundwith this release. Opening side one is the song '24 Hrs. Ago'. Its sweeping, metallic riff providesa menacing and theatrical tone that is taken on by the following track 'Beyond the Doors of theDark', which is another really heavy and powerful composition. 'Legions' then explores a grooved uppower metal sound, while the melodic number 'Strange Wings' sees Savatage dialing back on the speedand aggression of the first three songs. Side two then follows up with the instrumental 'Prelude toMadness' and the iconic title track that needs no introduction. Of the four songs that follow andconclude the record, 'White Witch' and 'Devastation' impress as well-arranged ballsy metal pieces,while the instrumental interlude 'Last Dawn' is quite enjoyable. Of course, many of the progressiveelements are still underdeveloped on this release, while the instrumentals occasionally feel likestopgap entries in a sequence of songs mostly dedicated to powerful riffing and vocal bravado.Nevertheless, the vocals of Jon Oliva are fantastic all throughout 'Hall of the Mountain King',while the writing and the arrangements are really strong. The quality of the entire album isindicative of how Paul O'Neill understood what the band needed to become an 80s heavy metal majesty.And despite its minor imperfections, this 1987 record remains one of the most important entries inthe band's catalogue.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — First it was FAIRPORT CONVENTION, but STEELEYE SPAN really planted the flag, and so were followed by worthy extenders in other lands, such as MALICORNE and TRI YANN in France, ANGELO BRANDUARDI and GIAN CASTELLO in Italy, CLANNAD and HORSLIPS in Ireland, MABSANT and PERERIN in Wales, CAPERCAILLIE and RUNRIG in Scotland, OUGENWEIDE and GALAHAD in Germany, MILLADOIRO and SANGRE DE MUERDAGO in Spain, and on and on. Most played a mix of trad/arranged and original/arranged trad style, such that, if you didn't already know, you'd be challenged to distinguish one from the other. They translated ancient poetry and prose into their native language and took liberties with the original melodies when they were known at all. I count myself among those who didn't realize that at least one Finnish group belongs in such select company, but given the breadth of Finnish prog folk, which is like THIS wide, I can't say I'm surprised by the presence or the quality of TARUJEN SAARI ("the island of sagas"), right from this debut.Led by the spirited and technically irreproachable vocals and woodwinds of Kaisa Saari, the hurdy gurdy and sundry from veteran TAPIO MATTLAR, twin violins, and a host of other folk instrumentation, this opening shot straddles all the aforementioned genealogical lines and draws a few of their own. When they choose a tune already well known to the type of people who would listen to this album in the first place, like "The Blacksmith", they give it a fresh spin, in this case it's more potent than the diva-ish LOREENA MCKENNITT rendition or the dirge like versions by STEELEYE SPAN when they were still finding themselves. They even tap the Swedes for the insistent "Margareeta". But the obvious standout here is Sinun Siniset silmasi" (your blue eyes), which merges flawless vocals, organic melody and guest cello.It's worth mentioning that for 30+ years a world beat group named VAARTINA has decorated their own room in trad oriented Finnish folk to an appreciative audience, but TARUJEN SAARI in unison pushes against the 4 (or however many) walls and thus, if not on the island of which they sing, can at least see it from their terrasse.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — A crisp, violin and guitar led prog act can't help but invoke a certain era of a certain UK prog monarch led by ROBERT FRIPP, and this instrumental album isn't unworthy of such a parallel, but this is mostly in the distorted icy leads and the jazz inflections. With no vocals and a tendency to prefer structured jamming over improv, not to mention a folk orientation that Crimson increasingly set aside after 1972, it would be as unfair to SCARLET THREAD as it is to an obvious mentor to stretch this analogy any further. A better comparison might be Montreal's TALISMA or, originating in the HACKETT school, MR GIL/BELIEVE or HARNAKIS. Among fellow Finns, perhaps AQUAPLAN but without vocals, at least for now.As I said, this is jamming but in a disciplined and repetitive way that generally works well enough and is nothing if not appealing to prog ears, though everything seems a bit interchangeable - throw in a guitar motif, enhance with violin, maybe add flute, then move on to another violin theme, and enhance with guitar, maybe add flute, and so on. Luckily these are all well orchestrated. The opener and closer seem to hit highest on the sustainability index, along with "Siipirikon Lento" (flight of the bird with the injured wing). More would emerge in the subsequent decade, with a few dramatic changes, so this is not one of those debuts that unwittingly doubled as a swan song. Mildly recommended, but more enthusiastically for certain listener profiles.

items.body: Review by bandtutu — Drowning Steps - The Bravery of a Tireless Mind: Book One1. The Angels and the PlaygroundThe Angels and the Playground is an excellent introduction to the album. I really like the way it begins to develop the character's story. One detail I particularly love is the sound of the pencil writing on paper. It may seem like something simple, but it really adds to the immersion in the narrative. Caio's vocals also deserve praise, as they fit the song's concept very well and help convey the emotions behind the story.The first three minutes are beautiful. The acoustic guitar is very well crafted, and the atmosphere at the beginning reminds me of moments from "The Moon Touches Your Shoulder" by Porcupine Tree and "A Pillow of Winds" by Pink Floyd. There is a nostalgic tranquility to this introduction that I really enjoy, with a delicate arrangement that allows each element to find its own space. The song progresses naturally, without rushing, and never becomes tedious.Around 4:15, we get an incredible transition. The guitar riff, accompanied by the keyboards and synthesizers, changes the whole dimension of the composition and creates one of the first major moments of the song. I really like how these elements complement each other. The acoustic guitar picking that comes in here, breaking up the rhythm, also deserves praise.At 6:30, the distorted guitar introduces a section that, although I understand its importance to the narrative and the character's emotional context, buy simply doesn't work for me. I really don't like the riff. I understand the intention behind the change and recognize its purpose within the song, but I feel another approach could have conveyed the same feeling in a better way. It's a very personal criticism, especially because the composition wins me back shortly afterward.At 7:37, another guitar riff comes in, accompanied by the synthesizer, and the result is excellent. The drums also deserve praise, as the changes in the groove give the composition more personality. I really like the bass's rich and distinctive tone, and for me, this combination works so well that it makes up for much of what bothered me in the previous section.At 9:07, after a very striking, almost ghostly break, the song moves into a section that reminds me of "Moonloop" by Porcupine Tree. Even though this is a relatively long passage, it never becomes tedious. The instrumental development keeps me interested and shows the band's ability to sustain extended sections without simply relying on the repetition of the same idea.At 10:47, a riff with a more metal feel begins to emerge. I can't quite define exactly what kind of sound it is, but I really like the change. It's the kind of riff I would even like to write myself, both because of its sound and the energy it carries. Just a few seconds later, at 11:02, another transition completely changes the emotional state of the song. The arrangement takes on a different dimension, setting the stage for one of my favorite moments of the track.The keyboards entering at 11:23 are simply incredible. The piano comes in with a very emotional quality, adding a special sensitivity to everything that had been building up until that point. This section really moved me, especially because of the way the instrument transforms the atmosphere without needing an exaggerated change in intensity. Thiago's work on the keyboards is fundamental here, showing how important his contributions are to the musical identity of both the song and the album.When everything seems to be heading toward a satisfying conclusion, the guitar comes back and creates a sudden shock that, interestingly enough, works very well for me. I don't see this choice as a problem, in fact, I really like the effect it creates.However, my biggest criticism comes right after that, at 12:27, when the previously used riff returns. I feel that bringing it back is unnecessary and slightly hurts the flow of the composition. In my opinion, the song had already found an interesting path toward its conclusion, and I didn't like going back to that idea.Still, I really like the grandiose effect created by the keyboards together with the vocals during the "Then we went up, then we went down" section. The combination has a lot of strength and fits the scale of the narrative, although the repetition of this passage became a little boring for me. The ending of the section, with the guitar delay, works well and sets the stage for the final part of the song.The final section is beautiful. After so many changes in intensity and instrumental passages, the song finally reaches a sense of peace that almost feels like a release. The atmosphere reminds me a lot of "Insurgentes" by Steven Wilson. It also gives me the same feeling of relief I get when "Raider II" ends and "Like Dust I Have Cleared from My Eye" begins on Grace for Drowning. After such a long emotional journey, it feels like you can finally breathe.Despite some choices that don't completely work for me, "The Angels and the Playground" is a very strong opening, with excellent instrumental moments, engaging dynamic shifts, and an atmosphere that contributes just as much to the musical experience as it does to the narrative.------------------------------------2. Fragments of a LifetimeI found this song quite interesting, especially because it takes a very different approach from the previous track. It has this kind of progressive folk-ballad feel, with a very atmospheric arrangement. The keyboard effects also remind me a lot of "Entangled" by Genesis, and I think they fit the song really well.I also really liked the ending, when the song starts to give you the feeling that something is going wrong. It's an interesting choice because it works as a lead-in to the next track, "The Nod", leaving a certain sense of tension in the air.I like the idea behind the lyrics, especially this moment where the character is searching for peace. Overall, it's a simple track, but it works really well within the story of the album. --------------------------3. The NodThe beginning of this song reminds me a lot of Opeth atmosphere. Then a very distinctive guitar riff comes in. I wouldn't necessarily say it's good or bad, but I understand the idea behind it and I think it works.I really like the part around 2:35, when a sequenced drum pattern starts playing in the background. I thought that was a very interesting choice, and it reminds me of some things Wilson has done. The drums also deserve some praise here; they give the song a lot of dynamics and help build that sense of tension without simply making everything heavy all the time.The bass solo is also really good, especially with the character's narration playing in the background. Then the heavy guitar riff from the beginning comes back, and this time I think it really gains more meaning and fits the song very well.I also really liked the synthesizer solo, which brings a different texture to the track. The guitar solo is good as well and works nicely within the composition.Overall, I think the song takes its time to show this depth and develop the idea further.----------------------------------------------4. Waiting for RedemptionThis is easily my favorite song on the album. It starts with a piano in the background and Caio's vocals, which once again deserve a lot of praise. I really like how the song gradually builds along with the lyrics, creating more and more tension as it progresses.The way the song keeps building gives me a strong Neal Morse vibe. I can't really say whether it reminds me more of Transatlantic, Spock's Beard, or his solo work, but there is definitely something about the way the song develops that makes me think of those bands.Around 3:50, a guitar riff comes in and fits the song really well. The effects also deserve a lot of praise here. They manage to create a completely different atmosphere and then return to the previous one in a very natural way, without making the transitions feel forced.This particular riff really reminds me of a riff from the bridge of "Weenie Beenie," from Foo Fighters first album. It's not exactly the same, of course, but the way the riff comes in gives me a very similar feeling.Then, around 5:15, the song goes through a complete change. Once again, it shifts into a darkness and more introspective atmosphere.Shortly after that, the synthesizer solo comes in, and together with the drums, it sounds incredible. Listening to it gives me a really good feeling, almost as if I'm going on a trip. And maybe that's exactly what the character is experiencing in the story as well.Then that heavy riff comes back, this time accompanied by a wah-wah guitar solo, and I absolutely love it. It's really spectacular. The combination of the riff, the guitar tone, and the wah-wah works incredibly well.A new verse then comes in, very well placed, followed by the return of that almost ghostly section, which keeps repeating.My only real criticism is that this final part starts to feel a repetitive. I like the atmosphere it creates, but I think it goes on a little longer than it should.Even so, this is easily the track that stands out the most to me. It has so many great ideas that fit together really well, and the way it moves between different atmospheres while maintaining the narrative is excellent.----------------------------5. Life Handed Me the MapThis is the song that closes the album. It feels like the character is expressing his gratitude for having finally found the path; the "map", that will allow him to reconnect with the fragments of his past.I really like the effects and the atmosphere of the song. There is something very calm and reflective about it, which makes it feel appropriate as the ending of the story.I also really like the detail of hearing him write again at the end of the song, followed by the sound of the book closing. I think it's a great way to bring the album to an end, especially because the sound of the pencil writing appeared earlier in the story. It gives the whole thing a feeling of closure, almost as if we've just finished reading the character's story ourselves.--------------Overall Opinion on the AlbumFor me, this is a work that shows how much the band has matured, both in their songwriting and in the way they tell their story. I really enjoyed the songs, especially the way the album manages to create different atmospheres and make them work within the narrative.The main highlights for me were The Angels and the Playground, The Nod, and especially Waiting for Redemption. Overall, this is an album that really surprised me and shows how much Drowning Steps has evolved. It's a record I definitely plan to listen to over and over again, because I feel like there are still a lot of details to discover.-----------My Ratings:4,3/5 8,6/10Congratulations for this excellent work.Caio Claro / vocals, acoustic guitar (1), guitars (2,5), Arrangements and Sound ManipulationFabricio Mendon�a / drumsLeonardo Gon�alves / bassMarcos Duran / guitars (1-4)Tiago Pierucci / keyboards, synthesizers, effects, organ, piano, Wah-Wah guitar (2), backing vocals (4), Arrangements and Sound ManipulationRobin Peachey / vocals (1)La�s Gonzalez / vocals (2)Erlend Viken / vocals (3)

items.body: Independent Polish musician Sławek Stróżyk released the single “Tylko Ty” (“Only You”) on September 18, 2026, through distributor Crave Digital. The track places Polish-language male vocals in a synthwave/electro setting with a cyberpunk atmosphere, and explores closeness as a source of strength while the surrounding world changes. “Tylko Ty” runs 2 minutes and 47 seconds at 120 BPM. Stróżyk wrote the composition and lyrics, performed the track and handled its recording, production, mix and master himself in his home studio using Reaper. The original music and vocals involved no generative AI. “Tylko Ty” previously featured on the “Synthpop Symphony” podcast. The single is available to stream on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. About Sławek Stróżyk Sławek Stróżyk is an independent musician, composer, guitarist, vocalist and producer based in Poznań, Poland, with more than twenty years of experience spanning session performance, recording engineering and sound design. His solo work brings together synthwave and electronic production with a wider interest in pop, ballads and rock. Stróżyk records in his own home studio using Reaper, taking responsibility for the complete creative and technical process from composition through to the finished master. “Tylko Ty,” released September 18, 2026, is his latest single under that approach. Stróżyk is currently working on his debut solo album, with material spanning pop, ballads, rock and synthwave, continuing the independent, self-produced method behind “Tylko Ty.”

items.body: Sydney-based producer Harry Klein released the single “Fleeting Moments” in 2026, a dark-pop track built from electronica, wave and witch house. The song centers on transience, and on learning to love what doesn’t last. “Fleeting Moments” runs 3:22 and carries a synthesized trumpet line, falsetto vocals and a glitch beat. The single adds to a run of 2026 releases that includes “Push and Pull,” “Only Ever Now,” “Dance Therapy,” “Sun Down” featuring Billsbry, “Wild Child” and “Refuge” featuring Just Jen. Klein is touring Europe with psych-jazz outfit Almost Toast and plans to release his second album, “On The Path,” in November 2026 after he returns to Sydney. Rex Pollard of Electronic Music Australia described Klein’s production in terms of the mood it builds: “It is clear to me that Klein contains excellent knowledge on formulating dystopian atmospheres with his production, encouraging listeners to exit reality and enter his dark, sinister worlds.” “Fleeting Moments” is available to stream on Spotify. About Harry Klein Harry Klein is a multidisciplinary artist based in Eora/Sydney who combines music production with visual artistry across audio/visual performances. His work moves through dark electronica, glitchy IDM beats and ambient textures. Klein released his debut album, “And Then There Was None,” in 2023. The record explores questions of relationships, community and social power, pairing experimental electronica and dance productions with melancholic pop songwriting. Three singles preceded it that year: “Running out of Time,” “Cut & Dirty” and “Accelerate,” followed later in 2023 by “Who Floats Above.” He has performed at Up Late at the Powerhouse Museum and the Brand X Artist Showcase, built an interactive sound installation at Wide Open Space Festival, played his festival debut at Waves Retreat Festival and collaborated with fashion label The Injury at Pitch Festival. Klein also works as Senior Technical Officer of Screen Arts and Photomedia at Sydney College of the Arts, where he teaches and mentors emerging artists. “Fleeting Moments” is the latest in a string of 2026 singles building toward “On The Path,” Klein’s second album, due in November 2026.

items.body: Kontravoid has announced an extensive European run for November and December 2026, combining support dates with Boy Harsher and Choir Boy, a stop at Hellsinki Industrial Festival, a series of headline shows and a final stretch alongside Los Angeles EBM duo Spike Hellis. The tour also includes three Polish dates in Warsaw, Kraków and Poznań. The tour arrives just weeks after Kontravoid released the new ten-track album “Sound of the Void” on 2 October through Artoffact Records. The record follows 2024’s “Detachment” and includes tracks such as “Mortal”, “Chances”, “Returning” and the title track. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid The first part of the European run begins on 14 November at Le Transbordeur in Lyon, where Kontravoid joins Boy Harsher and Choir Boy. Dates follow in Paris, Strasbourg, Frankfurt, Lausanne, Munich and Vienna. Boy Harsher’s own schedule confirms Choir Boy across these European shows. Kontravoid then breaks away on 21 November for Hellsinki Industrial Festival, where the Saturday bill also includes Gothminister, Das Ich, Ambassador21 and others. After further headline dates through Greece, Italy and Switzerland, Kontravoid returns in December for another run, this time with Spike Hellis. That section reaches Hamburg, Copenhagen, Berlin and then Poland, with shows at Mechanik in Warsaw on 11 December, Gwarek in Kraków on 12 December and Pod Minogą in Poznań on 13 December. The Poznań date is already confirmed as a Kontravoid and Spike Hellis bill, while the Kraków show has also gone on sale as part of the Europe Fall 2026 tour. Tour dates for Kontravoid 14.11 – Lyon, FR – Le Transbordeur * 15.11 – Paris, FR – Bataclan * 16.11 – Strasbourg, FR – La Laiterie * 17.11 – Frankfurt, DE – Zoom * 18.11 – Lausanne, CH – Docks * 19.11 – Munich, DE – Kesselhaus * 20.11 – Vienna, AT – Ottakringer Brauerei * 21.11 – Helsinki, FI – Hellsinki Industrial Festival 23.11 – Thessaloniki, GR – The Host 24.11 – Athens, GR – Death Disco 26.11 – Pisa, IT – Caracol 27.11 – Bologna, IT – Freakout 28.11 – Messina, IT – Retronouveau 30.11 – Zurich, CH – Xtra-Musikcafé 05.12 – Rotterdam, NL – Baroeg ** 06.12 – Paris, FR – Le Chinois ** 08.12 – Hamburg, DE – MS Stubnitz ** 09.12 – Copenhagen, DK – BETA ** 10.12 – Berlin, DE – Cassiopeia ** 11.12 – Warsaw, PL – Mechanik ** 12.12 – Kraków, PL – Gwarek ** 13.12 – Poznań, PL – Pod Minogą ** * with Boy Harsher and Choir Boy ** with Spike Hellis About Kontravoid Kontravoid is the solo project of Cameron Findlay, mixing darkwave, EBM, industrial electronics and club music. Findlay’s masked live presence has become part of the project’s visual identity, but the music stays built for direct physical impact: rigid bass sequences, heavy electronic percussion and melodies that often cut through the harsher production with unusual clarity. “Sound of the Void” is Kontravoid’s second full-length for Artoffact Records and contains ten tracks. Kontravoid’s North American tour with Buzz Kull ran earlier in 2026, and Side-Line covered the new album’s announcement in September (Kontravoid announces new album ‘Sound Of The Void’, shares single ‘Without’) ahead of its 2 October release (Kontravoid releases new album ‘Sound Of The Void’). About Boy Harsher Boy Harsher, the duo of Jae Matthews and Augustus Muller, enter the European dates with a new album of their own. “GET MEAN” was released on 18 September 2026 and contains twelve tracks. The record deals directly with grief, heartbreak and survival. It keeps the duo’s characteristic combination of minimal electronics, coldwave and physically insistent club rhythms. Their European tour begins in Lyon on 14 November and continues through France, Germany, Switzerland, Austria, the Netherlands and the UK. About Choir Boy Choir Boy began as the project of vocalist and songwriter Adam Klopp, with the current line-up also including Chaz Costello, Jeff Kleinman and Michael Paulsen. The band’s sound sits on the softer edge of the tour’s spectrum, built from dream pop, new wave and romantic synth-pop. In April 2026 they released the single “I’ll Always Let You Down”, written by the full band with Jorge Elbrecht and described by Klopp as an “anti-love song”. About Spike Hellis Los Angeles duo Spike Hellis bring the December dates back toward harsher body music. Their second full-length, “Successor”, was released on 7 August 2026 and follows their 2022 self-titled debut. The ten-track record includes “By God”, “Your Successor”, “Unwound (Get Right)” and “Entirely Mine”. It keeps the duo’s stripped, physical combination of EBM, industrial electronics and minimal synth. The duo describe their sound as “body music to hijack the amygdala.”

The ten-track release is Cameron Findlay’s second full-length for the Toronto label, following 2024’s “Detachment.” Coldwave, EBM and electro run through the record. About Kontravoid Kontravoid is the solo project of Canadian musician and producer Cameron Findlay, now based in Los Angeles. Before starting Kontravoid, he played drums with Crystal Castles in 2007 and 2008 and was a founding member of Toronto synth-pop band Parallels. His self-titled Kontravoid debut followed in 2012, released through the Minimal Wave label. He has toured North America alongside Buzz Kull, and the mask he wears on stage has become part of the project’s identity, a presence carried into “Sound Of The Void.”

items.body: Los Angeles darkwave trio Chalice Sect released its first EP, “Finis Initii”, on September 25, 2026. The four-track release combines two new songs with two previously issued singles, among them “Silent Fever,” released in March 2026. The EP’s four tracks move between post-punk, EBM and dark electro. Its title translates from Latin as “the end of the beginning.” Daniel of Chalice Sect describes the release as closing the project’s early period: “Finis Initii – Latin for ‘the end of the beginning’ – represents the closing of the first chapter of Chalice Sect. The EP brings together the remaining songs I wrote during that period but had not yet released, alongside the two previously released singles. These tracks were written over the past few years and belong to an earlier phase of the project, both creatively and sonically. Bringing them together on this release gives that era a proper conclusion while creating space for what comes next: a newer sound and perhaps a different direction for Chalice Sect.” Finis Initii by Chalice Sect The tracklist runs “Fire in the Sound,” “Silent Fever,” “Take Me There Parts I & II” and “Undefined.” “Finis Initii” is available as a digital release on Bandcamp and Spotify. About Chalice Sect Chalice Sect is a Los Angeles darkwave trio. The band released its debut single, “Violet Grey,” on January 20, 2026, followed by “Silent Fever” that March. “Finis Initii,” issued September 25, 2026 as the band’s first EP, gathers the project’s new and previously released material from that period into a single release. Press materials for “Finis Initii” cite Twin Tribes, Kontravoid, She Past Away and Molchat Doma as reference points for the band’s sound.

items.body: a-ha‘s second studio album, “Scoundrel Days,” turns 40 this year. The Norwegian band released the record on 6 October 1986 through Warner Bros. Records in the US, with WEA International handling distribution elsewhere. Recording took place in early 1986 at RG Jones Recording Studios in Wimbledon, south-west London. “Scoundrel Days” runs ten tracks and just under 39 minutes. Alan Tarney produced and mixed most of the album, while Magne Furuholmen and Pål Waaktaar self-produced “I’ve Been Losing You,” “Maybe, Maybe” and “Soft Rains of April.” Gerry Kitchingham engineered the sessions, with additional mixing by John Hudson. The tracklist runs “Scoundrel Days,” “The Swing of Things,” “I’ve Been Losing You,” “October,” “Manhattan Skyline,” “Cry Wolf,” “We’re Looking for the Whales,” “The Weight of the Wind,” “Maybe, Maybe” and “Soft Rains of April.” The album was preceded by the single “I’ve Been Losing You,” released on 22 September 1986, which reached number one in Norway and number eight in the UK. “Cry Wolf” followed on 24 November 1986 and reached the top five in the UK, Poland and Ireland. “Manhattan Skyline” was issued as a single in February 1987, peaking at number 13 in the UK. “Scoundrel Days” reached number one in Norway and number two on the UK Albums Chart, and was certified platinum in the UK, Germany, Switzerland, France, New Zealand and Norway. Rhino Records released an expanded two-disc edition on 6 July 2010, adding extended mixes, demos, B-sides and live tracks. About a-ha a-ha formed in Oslo, Norway, in 1982 as a trio of Morten Harket on vocals, Magne Furuholmen on keyboards and Pål Waaktaar on guitars. Warner Bros. Records signed the band, and a-ha released its debut album, “Hunting High and Low,” in 1985. The title track and “Take On Me” became international hits, the latter reaching number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 in October 1985. The band returned to RG Jones Recording Studios in Wimbledon in early 1986 to record its follow-up, “Scoundrel Days,” released on 6 October 1986. a-ha continued with “Stay on These Roads” (1988), “East of the Sun, West of the Moon” (1990) and “Memorial Beach” (1993) before going on hiatus. The group reformed in the late 1990s and released “Minor Earth Major Sky” (2000), “Lifelines” (2002), “Analogue” (2005), “Foot of the Mountain” (2009), “Cast in Steel” (2015) and “True North” (2022). The current touring lineup adds Karl-Oluf Wennerberg on drums and Erik Ljunggren on keyboards, both since 2009, and Even Ormestad on bass since 2015. Forty years after its release, “Scoundrel Days” remains the second entry in a catalogue that now spans eleven studio albums.

items.body: Claudio Dondo began making music in the late 1980s. This path eventually led him to Runes Order, the project under which he has released countless recordings on a wide variety of labels since 1992. He has now joined forces with the German label Dark Vinyl Records and, much like on his previous album, initiated a collaboration with Regen Graves. We are presented with a total of 13 tracks. While the influences are highly eclectic, they can largely be categorized within genres such as Cinematic and Krautrock. The inclusion of additional guest musicians adds further diversity—for instance, on one track, a saxophone creates a wonderfully dark, Jazzy atmosphere. I wasn’t surprised to find references to John Carpenter’s films, yet this album offers far more than just Cinematic soundscapes. From vintage drum machine tones to driving rhythms, and from organ passages to analog effects, this work has a great deal to offer. Add to this a variety of vocal tracks alongside the instrumentals, and the result is a fascinating work that keeps the listener firmly in its grip. This is a varied and accomplished opus containing a few real gems. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Bury The Fetus”: Bury The Fetus by Runes Order & Regen Graves About Runes Order & Regen Graves Runes Order & Regen Graves is the collaboration between Claudio Dondo’s long-running Italian dark ambient project Runes Order, based in the Genoa area, and Regen Graves, a musician from the same Genoa scene known as a member of the horror-doom band Abysmal Grief. Dondo started the project in 1988 as Order 1968 and renamed it Runes Order in 1992 with the cassette “The Dream Door”. His catalogue includes “La Seduzione Del Silenzio” (1994), “Room 39” (1995), “The Art of Scare and Sorrow” (2002) and “Fase XIV” (2019), drawing on the cosmic and Berlin School tradition of Tangerine Dream, Faust and Klaus Schulze. Dondo and Regen Graves first joined forces on “Falsche Fragen” in 2023. “Escape”, their second album together, followed in 2026 on Dark Vinyl Records, pairing Berlin School electronics with horror and thriller soundtrack atmospheres across the thirteen tracks reviewed here.

items.body: Arcana Magna Silentia Cold Meat Industry The fourteen year gap between Swedish neo-classical/dark ambient project Arcana’s As Bright As A Thousand Suns and new LP Magna Silentia was marked by halted reactivations, live reunions, and tremendous personal loss for Peter and Cecilia Bjärgö and their collaborators. It’s no surprise, then, to find them working in a register quite different from their last recorded material, though Magna Silentia‘s combination of Arcana’s earliest and most austere work and the technical prowess they’ve since accrued makes for a striking and affecting reemergence. Records like Thousand Suns and Raspail saw an expansion of Arcana’s acoustic side, augmenting their neo-classical side with folk threads which resulted in a sound not unlike mid-period Dead Can Dance. That degree of ornamentation has been stripped back Magna Silentia. Low, abyssal horns and drones accompany ritual drums whose earthy timbre carries real menace on “The Adversity Bell”, yet the melodic thread of the piece, carried almost exclusively by Peter’s wordless vocals, is far more frail and pained than those more bracing elements might suggest. And it’s in that tension, between the severity of a record which fittingly marks Arcana’s return to Cold Meat Industry (and everything that infamous label entails) and the full, crushing emotional register of real human grief and loss, that Magna Silentia shines. A sustained focus on funereal dark ambient drones and echoes is often the conduit for that tension. Dark ambient has always been one part of Arcana’s heady alchemy to be sure, but it’s never been given so much focus as it has here. The rich sound design and subtle but elegant compositional chops which guide “Somnia Intus” might not have been achievable for Bjärgö in the project’s early years, but are now well within his grasp and fit the record’s sober and enduring grief. While perhaps more abstract and less directly emotional, “The Obsidian Mirror” again finds Arcana wielding both metallic, industrial noise and contemplative tones in equilibrium (for a project which has always focused on atmosphere they’ve rarely felt “cinematic” in the way that term’s often deployed, yet there’s something of a classic cyberpunk cityscape in this track). For all of its pain and extremity, there are real currents of beauty in Magna Silentia. The mournful violin which passes through glowing chorales in “The Collapsing Of All Light” might not be as bombastic as some of Arcana’s earlier neo-classical works, but it’s as affecting as any of them. After their hiatus Arcana have returned to their roots, shaped by time and loss, but none the weaker for it. Recommended. Buy it.
