items.body: I had hoped to be seen by you Unbroken gaze like a sweet arrow Could you ever feel my eyes on you Bathing you in my desire Desire has a way of making the body speak before the mind has decided what to say: flushed cheeks, an aching chest, the unreasonable hope that somebody might feel a glance from across the room. In the video for Sacred Hearts, Gloria de Oliveira takes those private sensations onto the streets of Hamburg’s St. Pauli district, where barroom lamps, photo-booth portraits, and the company of women give longing somewhere to live. The song’s burning heart finds a fitting companion in the red lights overhead, while affection passes between its subjects through looks, laughter, and the small pleasure of being together. The Berlin-based German-Brazilian musician and visual artist shares the video for the third single from her forthcoming album The Lying Swans, due October 30, 2026, through La Double Vie and Cargo Records. Produced by Randall Dunn, whose work includes records with Anna von Hausswolff and Marissa Nadler, Sacred Hearts considers the exhilaration and anxiety of giving yourself over to another person, particularly when the body seems to have made that decision ahead of you. The opening guitar figures carry an almost medieval character, joined by bright, percussive tones with the delicacy of a hammered dulcimer. Matt Chamberlain’s drumming briefly suggests the forward motion of Kate Bush’s Running Up That Hill before settling into the song’s own gait. Deep resonant strings lend the arrangement weight, while synthesizers soften its edges and extend its peculiar, old-world atmosphere. The tones and melody evoke a folk ballad like Nick Cave’s The Weeping Song, with the spaciousness of a Western just beyond the song’s antique ornamentation. De Oliveira sings into that space with a delicate quiver that evokes Elizabeth Fraser, with a classical poise softened by the intimacy of her delivery. Lennard Zander’s acoustic, electric, and 12-string guitars trace fine melodic lines without disturbing the vocal’s tenderness; Arjan Miranda anchors the arrangement on bass, while de Oliveira, Dunn, and Úlfur Hansson add layers of synthesizer. The music leaves her exposed yet almost weightless, as if every declaration of love might tip her toward losing her footing. The lyrics measure desire through its physical symptoms, moving from fever and sleeplessness toward the hope contained in a hand’s touch. To be seen becomes as urgent as to be loved, and the repeated attempts to contain that feeling only reveal its scale. Yet, the song’s title draws on an image de Oliveira has carried since childhood, joining religious devotion to the unruly sensations of romantic attachment. “The Catholic image of Christ’s Sacred Heart – a heart literally engulfed in flames – has struck me since childhood.” “Of course it’s meant to symbolise God’s boundless and passionate love for mankind – however, as John Keats once wrote, ‘I am certain of nothing but of the holiness of the heart’s affections, and the truth of imagination’. And how does it feel to give yourself over to that affection and desire despite fear? With this song, I wanted to capture these seemingly contrasting sentiments.” Shot and directed by award-winning Turkish filmmaker Seda Kaçak, and edited by de Oliveira, the video stars London actress Mona Najma alongside Eva Rogalla. Kaçak follows the women through St. Pauli in handheld close-ups, catching them sharing drinks, posing for photo-booth pictures, and moving between daylight streets and richly coloured interiors. Superimposed faces and starbursts around the lights give these ordinary pleasures an enchanted quality. Conceived as a homage to the bond between women, the film offers an affectionate counterpoint to the song’s solitary ache: companionship makes room for feelings that can otherwise become overwhelming. Watch the video for Sacred Hearts below: A classically trained singer whose acting work includes Babylon Berlin and Christian Petzold’s Undine, de Oliveira released music with the darkwave and synthpop duo lovespells before her 2020 debut album Fascination. Her 2022 collaboration with David Lynch’s longtime sound designer Dean Hurley, Oceans of Time, followed through Sacred Bones. Across those releases, she has explored dream pop, ethereal wave, ambient music, and the influence of her Brazilian roots, alongside work for theatre, film, and London Fashion Week. Recorded in Iceland, New York, and Berlin, The Lying Swans extends those interests across nine songs concerned with trauma, perception, and the difficult return of trust. Its title invokes the myth of Leda, while its literary references include John Keats, Emily Brontë, Anne Sexton, and Milton’s Paradise Lost. Within that broader examination of love and illusion, Sacred Hearts holds open the possibility of affection despite fear. Listen to Sacred Hearts below or via streaming services, and pre-order The Lying Swans here. The album is out October 30, 2026, on digital, vinyl, CD, and cassette. items.body: …O sun, that healest all distempered vision, thou dost content me so, when thou resolvest,that doubting pleases me no less than knowing! -Dante Alighieri, Divine Comedy Golden Apes have spent more than twenty years making music for people who think a bass guitar should sound slightly dangerous, a baritone ought to carry bad news with dignity, and every decent chorus deserves at least one guitar line large enough to knock over the furniture. On The Sun Came Up Tremendously, the Berlin band sounds completely at home with that assignment. Ten songs move between post-punk, dark wave, gothic rock, dreampop, and bruised alternative rock, yet the record never feels like a display cabinet of influences. Golden Apes know this country too well for tourism. They have lived here. There is plenty of history in these songs, of course. You can hear The Cure in the open space around certain guitar lines, Chameleons in the upward sweep of others, Cocteau Twins in the gauzier passages, and the severe romantic machinery of Clan of Xymox when the keyboards begin closing in. White Lies, Interpol, Lowlife, and The Horrors, drift through the bloodline. Yet Golden Apes have reached the point where influence is less a matter of borrowing than instinct. Twenty-plus years will do that to a band. Eventually your record collection gets absorbed into your nervous system. The Sun Came Up Tremendously follows 2024’s Our Ashes at the End of the Day as the second installment in a planned trilogy, with material written across 2024 and 2025 and recorded at Thommy Hein Studios in Berlin between late 2025 and early 2026. Thommy Hein also contributes guitar, joining vocalist and keyboardist Peer Lebrecht, guitarists Maximilian Hennig and Stephan Schoenfeld, bassist Christian Lebrecht, and drummer Salomon Bosse. The production favors size without polishing away the pressure inside these songs. Basslines keep pushing forward, drums give the record a stern physical gait, and the guitars are allowed to bloom, bruise, and occasionally swallow the room. Farewell begins with a plaintive guitar that sounds as if it’s emerging from a dream, and an open space that immediately calls The Chameleons to mind, though The Horrors’ later grandeur also shows in the way the arrangement keeps adding height. It is a lovely opening, sad without collapsing into self-pity, and expansive without turning into marble-statue rock. Peer Lebrecht sings as though he has already accepted whatever the song is grieving, which somehow makes the ache sharper. By the time the rhythm section settles in, the track feels less like a goodbye than the long walk away from one. The Light (Inside Us) comes on harder. The guitars widen, Christian Lebrecht’s bass digs in, and the verses carry a conversational quality before the chorus breaks open into a shoegaze-heavy rush. The seduction of scale takes center stage: the chorus is huge enough to make a ceiling seem temporarily optional, yet the band keeps enough dirt in the guitars to prevent grandeur from becoming ceremony. This is music reaching for the upper rows while keeping both boots on the club floor. Milk and Poison turns inward and drops the temperature. Its opening feels like ripples on water with dream-pop textures, though the song soon settles into an anthemic ballad buoyed by these currents, sailing on broad synth pads, acoustic accents, surging guitars, and Peer’s low, expressive voice. He has one of those voices that can make a grocery list sound vaguely incriminating, and Golden Apes wisely avoid burying it beneath unnecessary decoration. The arrangement gives him room, then closes around him in slow degrees. Resistance is where the record’s architecture comes into sharpest focus. A resonant guitar figure opens the track, answered by a low keyboard tone, as hi-hats hiss at the edges and the bass builds steady pressure. The arrangement grows heavier until the guitars reach the emotional scale of mid-eighties gothic rock. Peer remains composed as the band swells around him, and that restraint gives the song its authority. Near the center, a clean, melodic guitar solo arrives with almost startling simplicity, offering a brief clearing before the vocal returns with greater weight. No pyrotechnics are needed; the song already knows where its gravity lies. At intervals, the drums break into splashes and the rhythm pulls back, leaving more air around Peer’s euphoric delivery. The measured bass, sober guitar tone, and baritone gravity recall Scottish cult band Lowlife, while the surrounding textures remain recognizably Golden Apes. Helion heads toward the same terrain as Clan of Xymox and The Chameleons, with traces of Joy Division in its resigned vocals and the stern drive of its rhythm section. An emotional barrage of drums and surging guitars carries the song forward, giving its sense of exhaustion an almost overwhelming physical force. There is something perversely satisfying about how controlled it remains amid all that turbulence. Plenty of bands mistake gloom for permission to wallow; Golden Apes keep pushing through it. It is the sort of song you want to hear live, feel in your chest, and carry with you on the walk home after everybody else has disappeared. Where the River Ran slows the pace and brings Peer’s baritone into Nick Cave territory. The drums begin with a plodding military tattoo, giving the song a processional character, while guitar and synth gradually stretch outward until the arrangement takes on a shoegaze breadth. The transition works because the band allows it to happen patiently. What begins in discipline ends in something far less contained. Evelyn (One Day) opens with a long sigh, which is about as efficient a piece of scene-setting as anybody could ask for. The resemblance to Lowlife grows even stronger here, recalling the Scottish band at their most wistful, thoughtful, and romantic. Dream-pop synth textures surround Peer’s voice, while dramatic splashes of guitar and percussion accent the song’s tender emotion, not unlike The Cure’s “Push.” Once again, Golden Apes take the form of a ballad and keep expanding it until the walls seem to move outward. The song swells like the ocean, its quieter passages gathering strength before euphoric surges of guitar and drums break across the arrangement. Their fondness for large choruses could become ridiculous in less experienced hands, but the rhythm section keeps the drama tethered to muscle. Radiation opens with a steady drumbeat and dirgeful tones before Peer’s rich, deep baritone bellows with unusual force, almost thunderous without losing definition. The chiming guitars and rhythm section pull back to give him room, though the melodic bassline remains palpable, felt in the heart and bones. With the song’s titular refrain, a surge of guitars seems to radiate toward the fingertips, giving its emotional release a physical reach. The drums then quicken in anticipation, and the guitars sweep in sustained arcs before the refrain returns, each repetition gathering strength from the space the band leaves around the voice. City Walls slows everything again, returning to the Cave-like gravity heard earlier. The drums drag with deliberate weight while a manic hi-hat keeps scratching at the surface, and eerie female backing vocals add an uneasy human presence around Peer’s lead. The song feels boxed in by design. Space exists, but none of it seems comfortable. Every instrument appears to occupy its own corner while the room keeps shrinking. Then comes Dreams (Gone By), opening with strange industrial textures before a weighty rhythm section and eerie synth tones take control, recalling London After Midnight’s Kiss. The percussion has real physical heft, but the gloom gradually recedes as the song opens into the brighter dream-pop romance of Modern English and Lowlife. Golden Apes carry that change with the emotional swell established throughout the album, letting the arrangement expand without losing the force of its darker beginnings. A brief pause for a wistful guitar chime offers some breathing room before the gothic dance rhythm returns, subtly brighter now, and the song surges again. As a closer, it gives the album one last change in texture, moving from industrial unease toward romantic release while retaining the emotional weight of the previous nine tracks. By this point, the record has passed through goth, post-punk, dreampop, dark wave, and broad alternative rock without sounding indecisive. Golden Apes can write a severe club track, a huge guitar chorus, a graveyard ballad, or a slow piece that sounds built for stained glass and bad decisions, and somehow Peer Lebrecht’s voice keeps the record unified. His baritone carries longing, isolation, regret, and the occasional flash of release without turning every lyric into a public execution. There is drama here, plenty of it, but the band understands proportion. Even at their biggest, they leave enough space for the songs to breathe. The Sun Came Up Tremendously is also the work of a band with very little interest in pretending they discovered any of these styles yesterday. Golden Apes’ long touring history, including appearances at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Castle Party, and Murder of Crows, plus stages shared with The Chameleons, Pink Turns Blue, And Also the Trees, She Past Away, Whispering Sons, TRAITRS, Then Comes Silence, and others, has given them the practical education that comes from watching songs survive outside the studio. The title may promise sunrise, though nobody should expect birds chirping outside a kitchen window. Golden Apes prefer their light complicated, filtered through regret, desire, bad choices, and the stubborn suspicion that survival can occasionally be worth the inconvenience of a journey through hell and back. The only way to reach dawn, after all, is through the night. The Sun Came Up Tremendously is out now through Icy Cold Records. Listen to the album below and order here. items.body: Progressive rock can be defined in many ways but one of my favorites is with the tension between a frenetic, jittery energy and sweet, soothing melody. Think King Crimson, where you never know which the band will choose from and often get both: the staccato, chopped up riff, or the dreamy, pleasing melody. This creates a tension, a contrast between the two sounds that, when wielded well, generates an inimitable energy and mood. Sans Froid are experts at doing just that, marrying dense, complex, unpredictable instrumentation and unexpected vocal phrases with a "classic" melodic approach. The end result is Back Into the Womb, an album that covers the spaces between heavy, muscular progressive rock and fragile, warm art rock."Go On", the track which opens the album, leaves us very little space before it introduces the first aspect of this sound. This is the track's excellent combo of the main guitar riff, punchy drums, and punctual bass. It creates that off-kilter vibe I mentioned earlier, that jittery feeling. The vocals follow suit but also quickly usher in the other mood, a more classical, melodic kind of approach on the track's first bridge. But here's the thing - that back and forth is not maintained. There is no A/B/A/B/C structure to this track. It gets smashed to pieces by this sudden turn that the instruments and especially the vocals take around at two minutes and fifteen. It's hard to overstate how much I love what happens there: the initially repetitive but then exquisitely explosive vocals, the deconstructed guitar line, and then the return of the big, muscular main riff.The entire album is filled with these ideas, refusing to choose one style and instead hopping between groove, experimentation, emotiveness, abrasiveness and more. Throughout, the vocals lead the way. They're incredible, again channeling that contrast we opened on. Their basic timbre is very sweet but it often gets augmented by a throaty, full approach that works exceedingly well with the album's basic groove. But, as evinced on "Go On", Sans Froid are happy to manipulate them further, sometimes casting them in sweeping, "traditional" choruses and sometimes chopping them up and deploying them in non-standard ways while at others setting them as a melancholic, emotive, gentle dirge. The result is that their sound is the centerpiece of the album, tying everything together, but never becoming obvious or background noise.Which also brings us, at the outset, full circle to the album's other brilliance: its production. Every instrument is meticulously placed where it needs to be and even on the album's busiest passages, every comes through beautifully. The bass is at the bottom but it never slips, always audible in its support. The drums hit very hard right where they should without overwhelming anything else. And the guitars are at time noisy and beefy but at others poignantly sharp and incisiveness. It serves to bring Sans Froid's ambition, which is substantial, to exquisite execution, bringing forth the musical vision in beautiful light. Fans of progressive rock know how hard this is to achieve and also know the joy of discovering an album which does this well, an intricate album whose sound matches its composition. Back Into the Womb is that and more, an album from a band which I knew nothing about that does everything I love progressive rock for. Back into the Womb by Sans Froid

items.body: 2026.10.06 音楽家のための心身サポートと熟達支援を提供する「ミュージック・エクセレンス・トレーニングセンター」 このたび東京・五反田に、音楽家のための心身サポートと熟達支援を提供する、世界初の教育プラットフォーム「ミュージック・エクセレンス・トレーニングセンター（トレセン）」が誕生しました。これは、楽器演奏における身体の使い方の研究で世界の先端をいく古屋晋一さんが中心となって立ち上げたもの。およそ四半世紀にわたる研究をもとに、科学とテクノロジーを駆使した独自のプログラムが組まれています。この未来を先取りするような「トレセン」を訪れ、古屋さん及びチーフコーチに最新の設備やプログラム内容について伺いました。 取材・文 取材・文 長井進之介 ピアニスト/音楽ライター 国立音楽大学演奏学科鍵盤楽器専修（ピアノ）卒業、同大学大学院修士課程器楽専攻（伴奏）修了を経て、同大学院博士後期課程音楽学領域単位取得。在学中、カールスルーエ音楽大学... 詳しく見る 扉を開けると、2台のピアノと共に複数のカメラやディスプレイなどのハイテク機器が並ぶ空間が広がる。ここは古屋晋一さんが代表理事を務める一般社団法人NeuroPianoが開設した「ミュージック・エクセレンス・トレーニングセンター（以下：トレセン）」。 5年間にわたり実施されたピアノアカデミー＊の成果を発展させ、音楽家のための身体教育とトレーニングに特化した世界初の施設だ。スポーツ界では、オリンピック選手を支えるトレーニングセンターや専門スタッフが存在する。一方で音楽家には、そのような仕組みがほとんどない。 「身体の故障やメンタルの不調によって演奏活動を断念する方は少なくありません。文化を持続させるためには、音楽家自身を支える仕組みが必要です」。そう語る古屋さんは、「文化のSDGsを実現したい」という。音楽家が心身ともに健やかに成長し、生涯にわたって演奏活動を続けられる環境づくりをトレセンは目指している。 ＊ピアノアカデミー：ソニーコンピュータサイエンス研究所が10代のピアニストを対象に、身体教育と芸術教育を包括的に提供するピアノ教育プログラム。現在12歳で活躍中のピアニスト・天野薫さんは修了生のひとり 演奏者自身も気づいていない身体の使い方を テクノロジーで可視化 核となるのが、古屋さんが研究と教育実践をもとに体系化した身体教育カリキュラム「PEAC（Physical Education for Artists Curriculum）」。「なぜその問題が起きているのか」という原因に着目したアプローチを行っている。それを支えているのが、長年にわたる研究とテクノロジーだ。レッスン室には、姿勢や重心移動、鍵盤の動きを計測するセンサーやカメラが設置され、演奏者自身も気づいていない身体の使い方を可視化できる。 別室にはAIを活用した練習システムを備えたピアノを設置。演奏すると、指先の向きや鍵盤への入り方などについて具体的なアドバイスが表示される。5年間のピアノアカデミーで蓄積された指導データを基に、一人ひとりに合わせたフィードバックが行われる仕組みだ。 さらなる別室には、「外骨格ロボット」と呼ばれる指のトレーニング装置が。指に装着すると、ロボットが自動的にトリルや特定の指の組み合わせを高速で動かしていく。その際、自発的な動きはまったく必要とされない。複雑な運動パターンが何の無理もなく繰り返し体験できるのだ。古屋さんは、「これは筋力トレーニングではなく、脳のトレーニング」だという。効率的な運動学習を促す研究から生まれた技術であり、長時間の反復練習だけに頼らずに技術習得が促される。今回は短時間の体験だったが、装置を外したあと、指の動きの軽さを実感した。 「外骨格ロボット」を指に装着し、習得したい指の動きを入力すると、ロボットが勝手に動いてくれる。「安静にしているだけで大丈夫。脳がちゃんと学習してくれますよ」と古屋さん （古屋晋一：ソニーコンピューターサイエンス研究所 東京リサーチ リサーチディレクター、一般社団法人 NeuroPiano 代表理事、ハノーファー音楽演劇メディア大学 音楽生理学・音楽家医学研究所 客員教授、東京音楽大学 特任教授、他） 「PEAC」に基づくレッスンを体験！ 具体的なアドバイスで音が驚くほど変わる 続いて体験したのが、「PEAC」に基づくレッスンだ。まず筆者がショパンのエチュードの一節を演奏。その後、チーフコーチの塩木ももこさんが背中側から小さなボールを当て、「これを押し返すように意識してください」と声をかけられる。ボールを押し返そうとすると、自然と腹部や胴体で身体を支える感覚が生まれる。その状態でもう一度演奏すると、驚くほど音の響きが変わった。同じフレーズを弾いているにもかかわらず、音に厚みが増し、楽器全体がよく鳴るようになったのである。塩木先生によれば、「下半身や胴体が安定すると、指先が自由になり、音も変わる」のだそうだ。 さらに指先の方向や鍵盤への入り方についてアドバイスを受けると、わずかな身体の使い方の違いが音に直結することを実感できた。そして何より印象的だったのは、「こういう音を出したい」というイメージを実現するための具体的な手段が示されることだった。 姿勢や重心移動等の測定データが瞬時にスクリーン上で図示される。演奏者自身も気づいていない身体の使い方が可視化されることで、「なぜその問題が起きているのか」が具体的にわかり、「こういう音を出したい」というイメージを実現するための方法が示される 古屋さんは、「私たちがやりたいのは芸術表現を教えることではありません。どんな音を目指すのか、どんな表現をしたいのかを決めるのは、先生やアーティスト自身です。私たちは、その表現を実現するための身体の使い方や学び方を支えたいのです。フランス料理にたとえると、ヴィシソワーズ（ジャガイモの冷製スープ）を作るのは先生方の役割。その前にジャガイモの皮をむくことが、私たちの役割なのです」と話す。 演奏家が健やかに、豊かな表現を追求できる未来を目指すトレセン。取材を終えて強く感じたのは、ここで行われていることが「表現を支える」ということだった。その挑戦は、音楽家と音楽文化の未来を支える新しい一歩となりそうだ。 ミュージック・エクセレンス・トレーニングセンター 学習者向けコース ◆カリキュラムコース：演奏に必要な身体の基盤をつくる スケール・アルペジオコース 和音・オクターブコース 芯のある響きコース ラインをつくるlegatoコース   コースに含まれる内容：コーチング、トレーニング、コンディショニング、レクチャー動画、リモートサポート、独習支援   月額 ：33,000円 システム登録料：11,000円（初回） スキル診断 ：別料金（16,500円） コース期間 ：6ヶ月（全12回）   ◆短期集中コース：身体の壁を突破する短期集中プログラム items.album: 山﨑健太｜『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』
items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 会期：2026/08/07〜2026/08/23 東京芸術劇場 シアターイースト［東京都］ 作・演出：岡田利規 公式サイト：https://www.geigeki.jp/performance/theater412/ 誰が舞台に立ち、誰が客席に座るのか。誰が誰を表象し、誰がそれを観るのか。『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』（作・演出：岡田利規）はそんな問いを改めて劇場へと持ち込み、そして観客に持ち帰らせるような作品だった。同作は岡田の東京芸術劇場舞台芸術部門芸術監督に就任第1作として上演されたもの。もともとはドイツのハノーファー州立劇場のレパートリーとして書かれ、5月に初演を迎えた岡田の現時点での最新作『Sliding Away』を、日本版の出演者・スタッフとともに新たに創り上げたものでもある。 タイトルが示す通り、舞台は映画を撮ろうとしているゾンビたちの撮影現場で展開する。登場するのは映画監督ゾンビのぽいぽい（東宮綾音）、俳優ゾンビのいいね（百瀬葉）、第5助監督ゾンビのまーしー（島田桃依）、第6助監督ゾンビのがーしー（石川朝日）、ゾンビ音楽家のげりま（福原冠）。しかし劇中で実際に映画の撮
items.body: 会期：2026/08/07〜2026/08/23 東京芸術劇場 シアターイースト［東京都］ 作・演出：岡田利規 公式サイト：https://www.geigeki.jp/performance/theater412/ 誰が舞台に立ち、誰が客席に座るのか。誰が誰を表象し、誰がそれを観るのか。『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』（作・演出：岡田利規）はそんな問いを改めて劇場へと持ち込み、そして観客に持ち帰らせるような作品だった。同作は岡田の東京芸術劇場舞台芸術部門芸術監督に就任第1作として上演されたもの。もともとはドイツのハノーファー州立劇場のレパートリーとして書かれ、5月に初演を迎えた岡田の現時点での最新作『Sliding Away』を、日本版の出演者・スタッフとともに新たに創り上げたものでもある。 タイトルが示す通り、舞台は映画を撮ろうとしているゾンビたちの撮影現場で展開する。登場するのは映画監督ゾンビのぽいぽい（東宮綾音）、俳優ゾンビのいいね（百瀬葉）、第5助監督ゾンビのまーしー（島田桃依）、第6助監督ゾンビのがーしー（石川朝日）、ゾンビ音楽家のげりま（福原冠）。しかし劇中で実際に映画の撮影が行なわれることはない。ゾンビたちは現場に集まったはいいものの、主要な俳優もスタッフもやってこないため撮影をはじめられない状況にあるのだ。かくして、時間を持て余したゾンビたちはゾンビが映画を撮ることに関する持論を交わしはじめる。 『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』東京芸術劇場（2026年8月）［撮影：銀色なつみ］ 冒頭からいいねは、ゾンビが人間を演じるための人間メイクをするのには3時間45分もかかる一方、「人間がゾンビになるときのメイクはもっとずっと短時間でテキトーに済ませたってオッケーってされてるんだから」その非対称性には許しがたいものがあるとぶち上げる。あるいはぽいぽいは「どうしてわれわれゾンビがわれわれゾンビのこと考えるのに人間のつくったゾンビ映画参照しなきゃいけないのか」と言い、「人間のゾンビ表象からわれわれ自由になれる日がいつしかくるようにと願って」「ゾンビの視点で描くゾンビ映画」をつくろうとしているのだと宣言する。 『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』東京芸術劇場（2026年8月）［撮影：冨田了平］ 非対称性というキーワードからも明らかなように、ここではゾンビの存在が現実世界におけるさまざまなマイノリティと重ね合わせられている。劇中に登場するゾンビという言葉の大半は、そのまま例えばクィアという言葉に置き換えても──「クィアの視点で描くクィア映画」というようなかたちで──成立するだろう。言及される問題は多岐にわたる。例えばゾンビが登場する映画はすべてがゾンビ映画という括りに入れられてしまうということ。ゾンビは本当は人間と同じように歩くのであって「人間のゾンビ表象」は間違っているということ。残念ながらそんな「人間のゾンビ表象」によってゾンビが「教育」されてしまっている側面もあるということ。しかし「問題は人間の映画監督のゾンビ描写が貧しいってこと」ではなく「ゾンビの映画監督が圧倒的に少なすぎるっていうのが問題のほんとの所在」であるのだということ等々。 そして話題は観客のことにも及ぶ。ゾンビの観客はどれくらいいるのかと。しかもこの問いは、劇場にいる観客に向けて発せられるのだ。さらに舞台上のゾンビたちはおもむろにゾンビメイクを拭い去り、自分たちが「映画を撮りたいゾンビ」を演じる人間の俳優でしかないという身も蓋もない事実を観客に改めて突きつける。そうして明らかになるのは、舞台上にも客席にも、このゾンビについての演劇が上演されている劇場内にゾンビはひとりも存在していないという端的な事実だ。 『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』東京芸術劇場（2026年8月）［撮影：冨田了平］ 『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』東京芸術劇場（2026年8月）［撮影：相模友士郎］ ともすればポリコレ的言説の演説会にもなりかねない（というかそうでなかったとはなかなか言い切れない）この作品が、チャーミングな飽きさせない上演として成立していたのは俳優たちの魅力に負うところが大きいだろう。そのようなかたちで問いを社会へと持ち込めることもまた、演劇の可能性のひとつなのだ。 この『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』という作品は、『消しゴム山』（初演：2019）から『リビングルームのメタモルフォーシス』（初演：2023）へと展開する脱人間中心主義を掲げた岡田の一連の作品のひとつとしても位置づけられるだろう。そのコンセプトは『消しゴム山』では例えば「モノのための演劇」というきわめてラディカルなかたちで実現されていたが、同作では再演を重ねるなかで、アクセシビリティをめぐるさまざまな取り組みも実施されてきたのだった。それは中心とされてきたはずの人間のなかにも周縁化された存在がいるのだという、当然でありながら日本の演劇界においては十分に目が向けられてこなかった事実に改めて目を向ける取り組みでもある。ノン・ネイティブ日本語話者を出演者に迎えた『宇宙船イン・ビトゥイーン号の窓』（初演：2023）もこの系譜に連なる重要な作品だ。 劇場で配布されていた『劇場に置くノート1』に岡田は次のように記していた。「舞台芸術の上演が現状よりももっと、観客の身体やその振る舞いが肯定されている場になる。観客の身体どうしがその存在を肯定し合っているという場になる。そしたらそれはイノベーションだとおもう。どうやったらそれは起こせるだろう」。このような思想は岡田がアーティスティック・ディレクターを務める舞台芸術祭「秋の隕石」のプログラムや体制にも持ち込まれている。2026年の「秋の隕石」は10月9日（金）から11月3日（火）にかけての開催を予定している。 items.body: 会期：2026/08/01〜2026/09/27 会場：水野美術館［長野県］ 公式サイト：https://mizuno-museum.jp/exhibition/2026-08-exhibiton/ （前編より） 展示されていたのは、連作のうち《神奈川 横浜遠景》と《鞠子 名物とろゝ汁》である。注目したいのは後者である。 《鞠子 名物とろゝ汁》（以下、「鞠子」）に描かれた鞠子（丸子）は東海道のなかではもっとも小さい宿場であり、現在の静岡市に位置する。名物であるとろろ汁の看板や茶屋の様子は、「東海道五拾三次之内」（1834）をはじめ歌川広重のさまざまな東海道五十三次に描かれてきた。従来の東海道ものでは、江戸から京都へと向かう方向に連作が組まれているが、東幸を描いた本作では京都から東京へ向かう方向で組まれている。また、宿場のすべてではなく7カ所しか描かれていないことは、それまでの東海道五十三次とはねらいが異なるのだと考えられる。あるいは、やむなく断念したのかはわからない。 「鞠子」は紙を縦使いしており、画面の中央下部3分の1ほどに消失点が据えられた一点透視の構図となっている。画面中央やや上に錦の御旗が掲げられ、それを先頭で担ぐ洋装の兵士、後ろに三列で複数人の兵士が続いている。行進の左右にはとろろ汁の看板がかかった茶屋が並び、その手前には膝をついて平伏しながらも、顔を上げて行進を眺める男女の姿がある。飾りのついた御旗の背景はぽかんとひらけた空で、画面下半分の描き込みとは対照的だ。そして、右上にタイトルとして「東海道名所圖繪」「鞠子 名物とろゝ汁」と縦書きされている★4。 ところで、消失点は前述したように画面下方に位置する。つまり、消失点は錦の御旗ではなく、それを担ぐ兵士の顔付近にある。右肩に御旗を担いでいることから、消失点そのものは肩口のあたりにあり、担ぐ兵士の顔と、その後ろを歩く兵士の顔が消失点を挟むように並んでいる。どの兵士の顔も俯き加減で、町人の顔と同じく簡素な線で描かれている。芳年が多くの作品で描いてきた、歴史に名の残る勇壮な武士、強い意志から行動に出た者の表情とはまったく異なっている。本作と、一般的に想像される芳年の作品イメージには落差がある。 芳年の絵の特徴は、無惨絵に代表される“ショッキングな表現”だけではない。躍動する身体を一時停止したかのようなダイナミックな構図設定と描写力もその特徴だ。歌舞伎における「見得」はパフォーマンスにおいて動きを止めてみせるものだが、芳年は静止した画面に、存在しない前後の時間と運動を思わせる。例えば後年の《芳年武者无類 源牛若丸 熊坂長範》（1883）に見られるように、はためく着物や頭巾、踏みしめる脚や薙刀の柄といったモチーフは、周囲の余白をこの直前／直後に運動して通過していく空間として見せている。また、タイトルや人物名のキャプションといった画面としてのメタ情報も含めて画面が構成されていることは言うまでもない。 このような運動の痕跡と予感で埋め尽くした描き方は、一見静かな画題である晩年の連作「月百姿」（1885-92）でも健在だ。どの画面も激しい運動を描いたものではないが、遠景の月と照らされる近景の関係、また人物の視線や姿勢が持つ動きが余白を埋めている。 本展のポスターにも用いられている《魁題百撰相 駒木根八兵衛》（1868）では、画面を眺める鑑賞者に向かって銃口が向けられている。メタ情報のグラフィック配置も含め、芳年の画面設計は画面内の移動のみならず、画面へ向かう視線にまで向けられている。可視・不可視にかかわらず、芳年の作品に対峙する鑑賞者はこうしたさまざまな運動を辿っている。 しかし、「鞠子」の画面内は運動に満ちているようには見えない。行進に向けられる町民の目線と、行進する兵士の伏し目がちな目線は交わらない。それでも動きとしては画面の手前に向かって彼らは進んでくる。その運動により、錦の御旗はゆっくりと揺れながら前進したことだろう。しかし、画面内唯一の行進という運動は、その手足の運動をもっとも感じさせない正面から構図が取られている。これはやはり、変わりゆく時代、なにかの終焉を象徴する場面であり、ほかの勇壮な作品とは異なる質のものなのだろうか。 （後編へ）※2026年10月7日公開予定 ★4──ジャパンサーチでは単色のものが掲載されているが、本展では多色刷りの錦絵（版元：大橋屋弥七）が展示されていた。特に兵士の洋装は、ほかの連作に比べると落ち着いた淡い色合いであった。筆者は軽度の色弱のため、写真が手元にない状態で色彩描写を行なうことは難しい。色彩が重要な要素であることは理解しつつも、本稿では記述できない点をご容赦いただきたい。 鑑賞日：2026/09/12（土）

items.body: Truth must be said from the beginning, I’m not, even a little, objective when it comes to John Coltrane’s last chapter in life and in music. Those two are inseparable in any case. Second truth is that this last period that starts roughly sometime in 1964, prior to A Love Supreme, and ends with his death is my favorite music. He and all his comrades, especially Alice, Pharoah, Rashied and Jimmy managed to create a body of music of transcendence –an ascension for the soul and deep meditation for the mind. My album of choice is this last live recording (where the aforementioned musicians are joined by Juma Santos and Algie DeWitt on percussion), recorded just three months before his death at the Olatunji Center of African Culture in Harlem, N.Y.C. In a quite symbolic move (the place: deep in an African-American neighborhood, the name: African Culture and tradition as a starting point) the music of the players, even though both geographically and in name still black, still jazz but free, is already a new entity. With this recording, one that the sound is not so hi-fi, Coltrane’s sound seems to be in the final stage of the total freedom that Ascension initiated. Listening to the unrelenting growls, howls and their thick wall of sound created by Trane and Pharoah, one could easily comment that the two tracks, Ogunde of almost half an hour and the total reconstruction of My Favorite Things that clocks in thirty four uncontrollably joyous minutes, are pure noise. This ferocious a la Ayler attack by the two locked in reeds brothers, provides a rough field, like a magic carpet flying in the air, for the others to give everything they have. And they have to give a lot to the not so big crowd attending, as their collective struggle to follow or lead at some points, or intertwine with small gestures like the polyrhythmic-not-so-rhythmic barrages by Rashied, the lovingly plucked piano chords by Alice and the even though not always audible, monstrous strength by Jimmy on double bass. Allow me to humbly comment that Coltrane’s music channeled everything in black tradition and went beyond that. He created his own tradition. You also don’t need me to say that this is an amazing recording. One that encapsulates all the stated goals by John Coltrane himself. Total freedom, love, myriads of feelings and a spiritual unity that could be the final Truth. If there’s something to think about, to question, it could be this: where could his music go after this? Did he, before even turning 41, reached a point of no return? @fot.isn Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: Out Of Your Head Records, 2026 Personnel - David Léon: saxophone, flute; Kenny Warren: trumpet; Stephan Crump: bass; Ches Smith: drums. Bassist and composer Stephan Crump, a musician of extraordinary passion and lyricism, put together a crisp, bright new ensemble for his latest outing, Passerine , a work of originals inspired by the various nesting techniques of birds. Relying on a frontline composed of Cuban-American saxophonist and flutist David Léon and trumpeter Kenny Warren, and pairing up beautifully with the resourceful drummer Ches Smith, Crump has something fresh to say. " Stuck " firstly evolves in a 3/4 time signature, displaying a big, round bass sound that shelters sharp unison melody. Léon narrates a story over an arco bass ostinato, while Smith explores toms and cymbal sounds with sagacity. There's a change of pace and texture for Warren's expressive solo, and the interplay between the rhythm team becomes more defiant, leading to a swinging passage before returning to the initial waltzing breeze. " Glide " is executed with a compelling rhythmic quality underneath—Crump incorporating effortless bass pedals, pizzicato routes, and cool grooves that find consistent support in Smith's nicely brushed skins. On flute, Léon stands out, drawing from melodic and harmonic minor modes in his improvisation. " Weavers " and " Twenty-Five " are warm meditative exercises where all members leave flowery scents in the air while rowing in the same direction. The former piece rests on a relaxed bass harmonic conduction that breathes at a challenging tempo, having charismatic, pure-toned unisons running atop. The latter is a shape-shifter that initiates with a sparse bass figure, understated drumming, a pellucid flute whose gentle dance emulates the chirp of birds, and introspective trumpet. Warren and Léon always take maximum advantage of their instruments to create dual melodic lines that feel luminous and often varied in shape. That's the case on " Fly ", a well-balanced 3/4 canvas painted with a certain wry melancholia. Breathable bass and brush work create space and smooth out the environment, culminating in a pulsating bass pedal point at the center of the outro vamp. With sensitive collaborative input from the musicians enlisted, Passerine is a point of departure and an embrace of transformation for Crump. It's also detailed with rigor without abandoning the freedom of creating spontaneously. The composer's sophisticated sound and gracious storytelling are filtered into the album's sequence. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Stuck ► 02 - Glide ► 03 - Weavers

items.body:
Bestards (理想混蛋) are coming back to Singapore.

Following their sold-out show last year, the Taiwanese band will reunite with fans at The Theatre at Mediacorp on 18 December, 7:30PM. Presented by CK Star Entertainment, 《不是因为天气晴朗才见面》 (BESTORY) will also stop at Zepp Kuala Lumpur on 21 November before heading to Singapore.

Formed in 2017, Bestards comprise vocalist Kidding (鸡丁), guitarists Jerry (阿哲) and Dillion (建廷), and drummer Look (可沛). Their heartfelt songwriting has earned them a devoted following of “Little Bastards” (小混蛋), alongside a growing presence on Taiwan’s live music circuit.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by CK Star Entertainment SG 🇸🇬 (@ckstar.sg)

The band’s best-known songs include ‘不是因为天气晴朗才爱你’ and ‘离开的一路上’ (‘Farewell’), which have surpassed 96 million and 58 million Spotify streams respectively. Bestards were also Spotify’s most-streamed band in Taiwan in 2024.

Their Singapore return follows the September release of their fourth full-length album, 偶像包袱 (MIMICRY). Arriving three years after their previous record, the album explores adulthood through questions of responsibility, expectations, identity, and life choices, expanding beyond the youth and romance that shaped their earlier work.

Among its tracks is ‘最后一个谎’ (‘One Last Bouquet’), written and composed by Kidding. Its music video crossed one million YouTube views within four days of release.

For the Singapore edition of BESTORY, fans can look forward to a mix of familiar favourites and new songs from MIMICRY.

Tickets go on sale on 13 October at 12PM SGT via BookMyShow, with prices as follows:

VIP: SGD208

CAT 1: SGD158

CAT 2: SGD138

CAT 3: SGD118

CAT 4: SGD88

Prices exclude booking fees. VIP tickets include a signed postcard and a 1:10 group photo.

items.body:
Rolando Luna is bringing the sounds of Cuba to Singapore.

The former Buena Vista Social Club pianist will perform with his trio at Capitol Theatre on 30 November, blending Cuban musical traditions with jazz improvisation. Presented by Vamp Productions, Rolando Luna Trío: Soy Cuba… y Más! begins at 8PM, with doors opening at 7PM.

The trio’s repertoire spans original compositions, Cuban and American standards, boleros, and danzones. Fans can expect familiar melodies reworked through fresh arrangements and spontaneous exchanges, drawing on Luna’s grounding in Cuban rhythms, jazz, and classical music.

Winner of the 2007 Montreux Jazz piano competition, Luna has contributed to more than 200 albums. His career includes ten years performing with Buena Vista Social Club and two decades accompanying celebrated Cuban singer Omara Portuondo.

Luna began his musical journey at 15, studying at Havana’s Amadeo Roldán Conservatory before Portuondo selected him as an accompanist. Alongside their international performances, he has built his own body of work as a pianist, composer, and arranger.

The Singapore show is supported by the Embassy of Cuba in Singapore, with the Foundation for the Arts & Social Enterprise named as its charity beneficiary.

Early bird tickets are available until 14 October, 11:59PM SGT, with standard pricing taking effect on 15 October:

Seated, theatre-style free seating: SGD79 early bird / SGD88 standard

VIP Terrace: SGD124 early bird / SGD138 standard

Visit Vamp Productions’ event page for tickets and further details.

items.body:
ALPHA DRIVE ONE member SANGWON is making an appearance in Singapore this race week.

The K-pop artist will join PUMA’s Own Your Speed campaign on 7 October, with appearances at 313@somerset and VivoCity as part of the brand’s driver events featuring Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Be A Hit 대박나자 (@always.beahit)

The visit follows SANGWON’s first collaboration with PUMA, which saw him front a campaign with Korean fashion platform MUSINSA. This time, fans in Singapore will get a chance to catch him in person as PUMA brings together K-pop, motorsport, and streetwear during Singapore Grand Prix week.

Running from 5 to 11 October, Own Your Speed is PUMA Southeast Asia’s largest motorsport activation in the region to date. The programme spans a pop-up experience, driver meet-and-greets, community activities, and race watch parties.

At 313@somerset, The Speed Station pop-up launches on 6 October, ahead of the following day’s appearances. Ferrari driver Leclerc and McLaren driver Norris will take part in meet-and-greet events on 7 October, with SANGWON joining the day’s activities at both malls.

The campaign also includes car community events at HyperDrive at The Palawan @ Sentosa on 8 and 9 October, before wrapping up with Singapore Night Race watch parties at Paulaner Bräuhaus Singapore on 11 October. A PUMA Tracker Night Run on 5 October kicked off the week’s programme.

items.body:
Stick Men are bringing their progressive rock explorations to Singapore.

The trio comprising Tony Levin, Pat Mastelotto, and Markus Reuter will perform at Singtel Waterfront Theatre on 29 January 2027 at 8PM. Presented by LAMC Presents, Tony Levin Stick Men – Live in Singapore will showcase the band’s unconventional instrumentation and intricate, rhythm-driven sound.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by L.A.M.C. (@lamcpresents)

Formed in 2007, Stick Men build their music around Levin’s Chapman Stick, Reuter’s 8-string Touch Guitar, and Mastelotto’s mix of acoustic and electronic percussion. Using two-handed tapping techniques, the string players weave together bass lines, melodies, and layered textures, giving the three-piece a sound that stretches well beyond a traditional rock trio.

Levin is best known for his longstanding work with King Crimson and Peter Gabriel, alongside recording and touring credits with artists including John Lennon, David Bowie, and Pink Floyd. Fellow King Crimson member Mastelotto, who co-founded Mr. Mister, brings loops, samples, and electronic textures into his drumming, while Reuter draws on a background spanning progressive rock, electronic music, and contemporary composition.

The Singapore date follows the September release of Let’s THRAK Again, the trio’s tribute to King Crimson’s 1995 album THRAK. Stick Men are touring the record across North and South America, Europe, and Asia, adding to a live history of more than 500 concerts in over 40 countries.

Tickets will be available via LAMC Presents, with sale details as follows:

LAMC members’ pre-sale: 7 October, 12PM SGT. Tickets priced at SGD98, SGD108, SGD118, and SGD128, with limited availability.

General sale: 8 October, 12PM SGT. Tickets priced at SGD98, SGD108, SGD128, and SGD138.

items.body:
Hearts2Hearts have released ‘ICONIC HEART (Korean Ver.)’, giving their Japanese debut track a fresh spin.

Out on 5 October via SM Entertainment, the single revisits the Jersey club-inspired sound of the original, pairing bright synths and bouncy beats with the group’s playful energy. Its lyrics explore the excitement of moving forward together, using youthful imagery to express a shared sense of possibility.

The track originally served as the title song of Hearts2Hearts’ first Japanese single album, ICONIC HEART. The release reached No. 2 on both Oricon’s Weekly Singles Ranking and Combined Singles Ranking, alongside No. 2 placements on Billboard Japan’s Hot 100 and Top Singles Sales charts.

Ahead of the release, the group debuted the Korean version live at Spotify CLOSER on 2 October, during a special concert presented in partnership with Spotify. They are also set to promote the single on Korean music shows.

items.body: Look at all those people! Everything seems bigger on Hour‘s newest album. There are fourteen people in the ensemble (four missing the photo shoot). The Bandcamp description is a thousand words long. The album is offered on black vinyl, colored vinyl, deluxe CD and promo CD. So why does Ghost Bridge sound so much smaller and more intimate ~ even more so than Subminiature? The answers are the arrangements and the brevity. On Ghost Bridge, the Philly ensemble led by Michael Cormier-O’Leary continues its slow shift from post-rock to modern composition. The pieces – and by extension, the instruments – are given more room to breathe. A half dozen tracks unfold in a concise 36 minutes. Late in the set, a vocal selection slows the pace to a pleasant crawl. Hour is still more Rachel’s than Low, but is carving out a niche at a pace similar to that of a stream cutting channels in stone. The title is taken from an “unrealized movie concept” about a disappearing and reappearing bridge. From this prompt, the album muses on tragedies, ghosts and the nature of the soul. Over a quarter of the album is devoted to the title track, whose very length suggests it bears the specter of post-rock. Solo piano is joined by light drums, then vibraphone, then all the other instruments in time, gathering like a crowd at a wake, forming layers of consolation, adding confidence and strength until the grief itself becomes a ghost. The end is a soft mist of notes, a few stragglers staying behind to whisper to the piano before they all go home. But where did it all begin? “Pearls” is the opening track, proceeding from a series of repeated notes to engage in happy permutations. Little sorrow can be intuited here; instead the starting point is a breezy, carefree day, filled with horse-drawn carriages and hot air balloons until the full stop at the three-minute mark, when darker clouds can be seen on the horizon: not yet here, but on their way. The pianist stumbles; the string players look up; the concentration of the percussionist is disrupted. The flautist resets the mood: the sorrow has not yet approached, so let us savor the now. The sedate ending sets up “Centralia,” a series of layered phrases that circle back and repeat like recurring thoughts or the motivational sentences of friends. Only after “Ghost Bridge” does “Sky Is Blue” emerge, perfectly placed as the first track on Side B, albeit jarring in the digital and CD versions. The lyrics, sung by Heeyoon Won, reveal it to be an extensive message from the great beyond, delivered by a loved one who is completely okay, filled with perspective, encouragement and hope. Should one not own the LP, we recommend moving “Sky Is Blue” to the finale. Given this sequencing, “So Long Without a Word” slips into the void at the end of “Ghost Bridge,” its melodic tones speaking directly to the soul, the full stop now at 2:00, followed by increasing energy and resolve. A third phase begins two minutes later with insistent, cinematic strums, then a playful series of shifts, jazz to chamber and back, like a playground ball. “Sonny” returns the timbre to post-rock and the mood to reflective yet ebullient, the ghost bridge now reappearing, the path between heaven and earth secure. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Watch an exclusive premiere of the film of Ava Rasti’s The River, first performed as part of the 2025 Semibreve festival. The River by Iranian-born Berlin-based composer Ava Rasti was commissioned by Portuguese festival Semibreve and first presented on 25 October 2025 at the Capela Imaculada do Seminário Menor in Braga. The performance brought together Rasti and a string quartet composed of Filipa Abreu (violin), Vânia Oliveira (viola), Tiago Mendes (cello) and Catarina Coelho (cello). The work takes the Piave river in northern Italy as its inspiration, a landscape in which the present is intertwined with the traces of wars and violence from its past. Rasti constructs these fragmented memories, recontextualised and transformed into sounds. Wire subscribers can read Claire Sawer's review of Semibreve 2025 here.

items.album: [2View] Maps and Diagrams’ beneath still stars (handstitched*) & returning light (Home Normal)
items.excerpt: Two decades removed from the clockwork IDM of Polytuft-Tech, Tim Martin’s returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) find him stripping everything back to drift, texture, and quietly resonant melody, resulting in two companion albums that feel less like separate releases than different sides of the same long, unhurried thought.   Companion pieces, two sides of the same drift beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagrams   Tim M
items.body: Two decades removed from the clockwork IDM of Polytuft-Tech, Tim Martin’s returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) find him stripping everything back to drift, texture, and quietly resonant melody, resulting in two companion albums that feel less like separate releases than different sides of the same long, unhurried thought.   Companion pieces, two sides of the same drift beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagrams   Tim Martin has been Maps and Diagrams since the early 2000s, and the entry point for a lot of people into his catalog is Polytuft-Tech, released in 2003 on Expanding Records, an album that got filed under IDM, ambient, and glitch at a moment when those three words together still meant something specific and rigorous. That record ran on clicky drums that whirred like clockwork under warm, streamlined melodies. It landed near the tail end of IDM’s most experimentally saturated period, right as the genre itself was quietly transitioning into whatever came next, and it stands as one of the more melodically generous statements from that stretch. Both returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) are nowhere near that record sonically. Drums are gone almost entirely. Glitch has been replaced by drift. But it’s still unmistakably Tim, the same restrained, resonant signature that’s followed him through two decades of output, just aged into something quieter. Both albums arrive within weeks of each other on different labels with different histories attached. returning light is Home Normal‘s second release from Tim this year, following tone isolation, his actual debut on the label despite Home Normal running for over seventeen years, a gap explained by the fact that Tim‘s earliest UK work went through Nomadic Kids Republic, Home Normal‘s sister label, back in 2011 with Lights Will Call On You and The Town Beneath The Sea. beneath still stars comes out on handstitched*, the label Tim runs himself, which has carried his more private and experimental output for years alongside releases like In Circles. One album through someone else’s curatorial lens, one through his own. That distinction matters more than it initially seems to. Ambient releases should never get judged track by track in isolation. The genre works as a collective experience, an album like this either builds a sustained emotional environment across its runtime or it doesn’t, and no individual piece can really save or sink that outcome on its own. What matters more is whether the melodies that surface actually resonate, whether they invoke something specific rather than just occupying space. Both of these records succeed at that, though they do it through slightly different means. “ArcWorld-6.4 Rev.42 [sgl.break]” from beneath still stars is one of the more fascinating pieces across either release, another example of the part A / part B structure that’s shown up in other reviews recently. It connects two ideas without part B ever feeling like a continuation of part A. Instead it functions as an introduction to something entirely different, and the transition is peaceful in a way that most of this album is. The track titles throughout beneath still stars read almost like technical drafts, numbered revisions, hertz values, file extensions in brackets like [static] or [lost.wav] or [mem.void]. That naming isn’t arbitrary. It reads like an iteration system, drafts selected and refined specifically rather than titled decoratively after the fact. “Raddius.ocean-IX [r.36-04hz]” is another two-part piece, but this one connects rather than diverges, a drone-like melodic note giving way to a dreamlike synth tuned to a specific frequency, which the title tells you outright. Intentional down to the hertz. “beneath still stars and returning light aren’t competing statements, they’re companion pieces, two sides of the same drift, released close enough together that they start to feel like one long, unhurried thought that just happened to get split across two labels.” ~J. Batista A different level of drone entirely :: returning light sits in the same emotional register but sounds noticeably different sonically. There are small clicks and glitches scattered through certain tracks, and the pads and atmospheres carry a different weight than what’s happening on beneath still stars. “falling rainbows” uses static hits inside its pad environments to create reverbed textures that read almost like snare hits, except Tim‘s building that rhythmic tension entirely out of pad effects and reverb rather than anything resembling a drum sample. “just moving” introduces keys that sound almost like distortion at first before resolving into something prettier the longer you sit with it, a different level of drone entirely, since nothing here holds on a single note. There’s room for other melodies to form and enter, and they do. “somewhat virtual interactions” is a favorite, what sounds like a distorted “ahhh” vocal fragment sits so subtly in the mix that it changes the character of the pads around it, and there are field recording glitches scattered throughout that open up real space inside the track. “Open Water” plays almost like an audio representation of a shishi-odoshi—that traditional Japanese bamboo water fountain that fills, tips, empties, and resets in a slow repeating cycle. Tim‘s using effects here the same way that device uses gravity and water, building a soft, cyclical sense of rhythm entirely out of texture rather than percussion. “ouvertures” closes the album starting soft and distorted, and around the 3:55 mark a low humming frequency starts creeping in that sounds baked into the synth itself, eventually rolling and degrading the audio as the track winds down. A genuinely cool effect to end on. “Tim Martin has landed somewhere his younger self probably wasn’t building toward. Whether that’s evolution or just where two decades of making ambient music eventually deposits a person is hard to say, and probably doesn’t matter.” ~J. Batista There’s a version of this review that picks a favorite between the two records. That version would be missing the point entirely. beneath still stars and returning light aren’t competing statements, they’re companion pieces, two sides of the same drift, released close enough together that they start to feel like one long, unhurried thought that just happened to get split across two labels. beneath still stars is the more clinical of the pair. Drafted, revised, numbered like lab notes, every track title reading like a version history for a synth that never stops evolving. Twenty years removed from Polytuft-Tech‘s clockwork drums and whirring percussion, Tim Martin has landed somewhere his younger self probably wasn’t building toward. Whether that’s evolution or just where two decades of making ambient music eventually deposits a person is hard to say, and probably doesn’t matter. These two records don’t argue for themselves. They don’t need to. They just sit there, patiently, until you notice forty minutes have passed and you’ve barely moved. Home Normal got the warmer half. handstitched*—Tim‘s own label, his own house, got the rawer, more exacting one. He gets to have it both ways. So does anyone who sits with both records long enough to stop telling them apart. beneath still stars is available on handstitched* and returing light is available on Home Normal. beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagramsThe post [2View] Maps and Diagrams’ beneath still stars (handstitched*) & returning light (Home Normal) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Anyankofo means friends in Fante, and the Danish seven-piece Total Hip Replacement have been collecting them in Ghana since a mini-tour there in 2013. In the winter of 2021 they formed a nine-piece band in Accra with Ghanaian highlife, reggae and gospel musicians and gave it that name, which also titles the album the group recorded at Kwame Yeboah‘s Kwashibu studio, released in 2022. A later trip to Ghana took them to Kumasi, the Ashanti capital and one of highlife’s strongholds, and a week of jamming there with players from Frafra gospel singer Florence Adooni‘s band and with Nsoroma of Accra highlife band Santrofi produced “The Search”. It is the latest single ahead of the album Ehum, and the band say it holds on to the improvised feel of the jams. The song is about hunting for purpose in a society that keeps speeding up, where the pressure to get ahead alone costs people their connection to each other. Singer and trombonist Victor West Hosbond fronts the band’s horn section, the signature of their sound, and on this single it rides a highlife rhythm. The band describe the mood they chased as “the hopeful spot between melancholy and euphoria“. They filmed the video over a couple of days at an old farmhouse in France during this summer’s tour, with Nell Le Corre behind the camera. Ehum, which the band translate as storm, comes out on 27 November with Ivorian reggae singer Tiken Jah Fakoly among the guests. A West African run through Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana opens the tour, then Danish dates follow from February into April, among them ALICE in Copenhagen on 26 February and Aarhus on 27 March. Stream “The Search” HERE and pre-order Ehum through THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Total Hip Replacement – The Search appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 990Frost* is a progressive rock band, a neo-prog super group that was formed in East Sussex, England, in 2004. Frost* was founded by songwriter, producer and musician Jem Godfrey, who is better known to the wider world for his work creating chart topping pop hits, when he made a conscious decision to return to his own musical past writing and playing progressive music. After writing and recording material on his own for several months and contacted several English well known musicians. Their debut studio work "Milliontown" was released in 2006. In 2008 they released their second one "Experiments In Mass Appeal". The third one "Falling Satellites" from 2016 will be the subject of the review.Although the band has remained true to the neo-prog style, the line up changes have brought some changes to the band's sound. The keyboards now play a more dominant role and since the guitar part has also been reduced, "Falling Satellites" seems smoother than its predecessors. It has little in common with "Milliontown", apart from the general style. "Experiments In Mass Appeal" gives a better indication of the direction. But with "Falling Satellites" Jem is still going one step further. Here we have nice prog and sophisticated pop with a lot of drive and a good feel for melodies with a catchy nature. The band seems genuine with a lot of fun with what they do presenting themselves confidently.So, "Falling Satellites" is the third studio album of Frost* and that was released in 2016. The line up on "Falling Satellites" is John Mitchell (vocals and guitar), Jem Godfrey (vocals, keyboards, electric and lap steel guitars and Chapman Stick), Nathan King (bass guitar) and Craig Blundell (drums). "Falling Satellites" also had the participation of Tori Beaumont (vocals), Joe Satriani (guitar) and Mark Knight (violin), all as guest artists."First Day" is a very short track. It begins the album with an ominous orchestration and a spacey ambience. It provides an atmospheric introduction that sets the ambient tone to the album. "Numbers" is a great track, an enjoyable rocker with a nice lilt to it that sets the upbeat tone of the album. It has a lot of depth and a lot going on. The vocals are layered perfectly on top of the instruments and backing tracks. "Towerblock" is easily the standout track on the album due to its level of experimentation and complete unconventionality within the scope of this sub-genre. It embraces their pop and electronic sensibilities and reflective lyrics into something that feels modern, but also classic. "Signs" has love lyrics with Mitchell on the lead vocals. This is arguably the most pop-oriented track we've heard from the band. It's another strong and heartfelt song that wouldn't sound out of place on either of their previous albums. "Lights Out" is a sort of ballad with pop infusions, a lovely tune with some great guest vocals by Tori singing along with Godfrey. It's a fantastic power ballad, a nice break in the middle of the album, to prepare us for the epic second half. "Heartstrings" is a solid rocker with great hooks and massive synthesisers. It oscillates between fiery futuristic hostility and calm, and the pop sensibilities. It has an ending that partially serves to transition into the following track. "Closer To The Sun" is more somber overall, a very dance-like track that brings the focus back around to the ambient pop vibes of "Lights Out". It's a track of beautiful, atmospheric and poppy post-rock, completed with great guitar and keyboard solos. "The Raging Against The Dying Of The Light Blues In 7/8" is the longest track on the album. It's full of energy outbursts and soft moments. It's a highly enjoyable hard rock song, energetic and captivating. It's a blistering track that should more than satisfy those looking for the pure prog on this album. "Nice Day For It..." is another dynamic and harmonically rich rocker. This is a real progressive rock track which contains certain musical elements you also hear on "First Day" and "Heartstrings". It's another track with some heavy "Milliontown" influence, being mostly instrumental. "Hypoventilate" suggests some kind of a sequel to "Hyperventilate" of "Milliontown". It's a very short track like "First Day". This is a transitional track that leads us into the last track. "Last Day" is a soft, lovely piece only containing vocals and piano. It obviously reimagines the sentiments of "First Day" to give the full-length a sense of meaningful conceptual continuity.Conclusion: With "Falling Satellites", Frost* has managed to create a beautiful and entertaining album that cannot really deny its pop origins. The basic ideas of the pieces and the melodies can often be imagined as pop songs, but it's an album that is progressive above all because of its clever mix. Godfrey proves himself to be a great producer and true keyboard wizard and he also cuts a good figure as a singer. Together with his top-class accompanists, he turns "Falling Satellites" into a real fantastic bundle of energy that can be described as an unexpected surprise coup. It's an exciting, always surprising album, on which there is a lot for prog lovers to discover, even if it can never really keep up with the two strong previous albums. It's undeniable that there is a pop influence on "Falling Satellites". In many ways, Frost* has once again redefined what is "modern" prog and they've done it with gusto and pomp and a smile on their faces.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — Truly mind blowing album. Arguably one of the most manifold records from the dusk of that decade. HIGH TIDE have been one of the most important underground rock acts of that era. This album really blew my mind the first time I heard it. I almost did not believe that it released in 1969. Very few bands were so heavy back then. HIGH TIDE is so damn heavy, it really pisses me off that I can't recall a single magazine or online "list" of proto-metal bands that mentions these guys. You can find fragments of early doom in songs like "Futilist's lament" & "Missing out". You can hear neoclassical influences on the guitar riff on "Walking down their outlook". Also, on the same song, listen carefully the guitar lick on 2:20 (Judas Priest anyone?!?!?). And that violin... Majestic. Enchanting. Listen to "Pushed, but not forgotten". Amazing stuff, honestly. Some people may say that the [&*!#]ty production fits with the music and the atmosphere, I say it steals the music's grandeur.

items.body: Review by memowakeman — Review originally posted at www.therocktologist.comA third exquisite offering. The talented Italian quartet Aether is back with an incredibly solid, mature, refined, and creative album, one that fans of jazz fusion, progressive rock, and music that appeals to the senses will enjoy from beginning to end. Across 43 minutes and six tracks, the musicians treat us to a series of sonic landscapes that range from relaxing to frenetic, from atmospheric to deeply sensory, moving seamlessly between rock, post-rock, ambient, and classical music. It all begins with "Oort Cloud," whose opening seconds are atmospheric and otherworldly, creating a contemplative, dark mood. Little by little, new elements and sounds emerge, making you feel as though you are floating through space, caught somewhere between uncertainty and curiosity, until everything erupts at the 2:30 mark and a new rhythm takes over, retaining that dark sound that at times reminds me of early-70s King Crimson. As the minutes go by, the band introduces more colors, with the keyboards becoming a crucial element. Nevertheless, the atmospheres created by the bass, guitar, and drums come together to form a truly fascinating sonic experience. Next comes "Vogon," where the bass maintains a steady pulse while the guitar, keyboards, and drums appear here and there, gradually moving from uncertainty toward a sense of resolution as a distinctly jazzy melody begins to take shape. The very distinctive voice of the theatrical Claudio Milano emerges to recite a poem, creating one of the album's most unique moments. Shortly after his voice fades away, the music explodes, and jazz gives way to rock, with Andrea Ferrari's guitar charging forward like a whirlwind of emotions, compelling you to move and simply enjoy the music. The sonic landscapes shift in fascinating ways on "Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres." It begins by creating spacious, otherworldly soundscapes that, after two and a half minutes, take on an almost psychedelic essence, thanks first to the hypnotic bass of Andrea Grumelli, who guides the way as the guitar, synths, and drums deliver a daring and wonderful blend of space rock and jazz. This is one of my favorite tracks on the album. "La M�lancolie Du Petit Prince" features Andrea Serino's piano as the central element and guiding force of this literary-inspired passage. Beyond the blend of jazz and classical music brought to life by the piano, I love the fretless bass and its wonderfully fluid, graceful notes. I am also particularly fond of the deliciously sensory percussion Matteo Ravelli plays at the beginning, which he later contrasts with his electronic devices. Another majestic moment arrives with "Panta Rei." Its eight minutes unleash the quartet's imagination and creativity, showing us that after three studio albums, these musicians understand one another exceptionally well and flow together naturally, not only as accomplished instrumentalists but, more importantly, as a band. And although there are several darker, denser moments, I love the balance they achieve, as we suddenly find ourselves immersed in passages that feel bright and full of promise. At one point, they even reminded me of Focus. And yes, progressive rock is very much present here. Finally, the album reaches its brilliant conclusion with "Swerve." Over the course of its ten minutes, Aether delivers the climax of the entire work, a clear testament to the evolution of their sound and their boundless creativity. The band brings together a rich mix of genres and emotions, allowing listeners to immerse themselves in progressive passages, profound atmospheres, and enveloping, emotionally charged textures. The rhythm and intensity gradually build from the halfway point onward, creating a sonic spectrum that makes you want to move with the music, feel it, savor every moment, and truly make it your own. Congratulations to Aether on such a solid release. I absolutely loved it.

items.body: Review by Logan — Looking Beyond The Beautiful Space Out in the CountryThe short-form record tends to work on a different logic than a full LP. I value EPs that carry their own weight as intentional, self-contained pieces rather than just acting as a way to repackage existing music for sale.Much like a short film, an EP can use its brevity to settle into a specific mood or texture, without needing to extend those ideas across the length of a full studio album.Godspeed You Black Emperor!'s Slow Riot for New Zero Kanada does this well, letting tracks like "Moya" and "BBF3" create a heavy and distinct presence in under thirty minutes. Boards of Canada seems to approach the format similarly. A record like In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country does not feel like leftover tracks -- it works as an independent soundscape where the brief runtime is used for deliberate atmosphere.An important aspect of In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country is that these tracks do not appear on other major releases, which makes the EP an essential piece of their discography rather than a minor supplement. It stands out as one of my very favourite EPs. Listening to it highlights a beautiful and mysterious ambient density built on a sort of melancholy, discomforting and comforting nostalgia.I especially adore the tracks "Kid for Today" and "In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country" but I think the whole record is superb taken as a whole. "Zoetrope" did not at first appeal much, but during consecutive listens I got how its minimalist ambience worked with and added to the rest of the release. It helps to demonstrate how their use of repetitive, cyclical structures can reveal deeper qualities when one sits with the textures over a period of time. That highlights to me how a track can reward patience.I give it 5 stars as one of my most essential EPs.

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — One of my favorite albums of 1969 hands down. So many styles of music one can find here. Blues, psychedelia, jazz, classical, rock. All of them combined to provide a sample of proto-prog in the late 60s British scene. Songs like "Isadora", "Waterways", "Bathers", "Moth" are majestic. Geoff Nicholson delivers some really beautiful and heart-warming vocal harmonies. But, Dave Arbus steals the show here. With his electric violin and his flute, he blesses our ears with some enchanting melodies. This album really could be close to perfect, if it weren't for those free jazz/improvisations on the songs "Centaur woman" & "In the stable of the Sphinx" which in my opinion kind of mess up a little bit the whole atmosphere of the album.Nevertheless, this is a really strong album, that the fans of the early prog rock era should check out.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — When I first heard a few tracks by this Finnish band, I gradually realized that what captivated me was the blend of King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard's irreverence toward musical genres, an approach that, while experimenting with them all, still respects them and follows their rules. I was also reminded of The Cardigans: a mix of tradition and the past, combined with a freshness where technology, jazz, and a unique brand of pop came together. Their debut album opens on a serious note with classical piano and violins, key elements of their sound, and the magical voice of Eeva Rajakangas; on the track "T�nne saakka ei aurinko paista," she recites the lyrics, creating a powerful and truly special moment. Kadenssi reveals the strong influence of Nordic traditional music, austere, profound, and almost sacred, and Celtic music, danceable and luminous, sharing a common thread in that both border on the mystical.With the fourth track, Kahdeksas p�iv�, rock and modernity enter the mix, while maintaining that distinctive nine-piece lineup, featuring two violins and a saxophone, where the true fusion begins. A folk atmosphere, driven by the flute, occasionally evokes the folk-rock sound of Jethro Tull; yet, modern drum loops and Eeva's spoken-word vocals merge into a blend of jazz, funk, and punk. Add to this a dissonant chorus and a distorted, psychedelic cabaret vibe, and it feels as though we are witnessing a whole new album within the album itself."Planeetta" plays with space and silence; Eeva's voice sings and then recedes, as does the piano, eventually revealing a jazz-infused atmosphere driven by violins and saxophone, lending the track a distinctive character. It then returns to Celtic roots, yet approaches them not in the traditional manner, but with a rock and funk sensibility, featuring a syncopated, irregular rhythm."08" continues with the distinctly postmodern vibe created by Eeva's spoken vocals, almost prophetic in tone, which has become a signature, recognizable style for the band. Just as Pessi Jouste's classical training is evident in the violin work, Aino Kallio's influence shines through on the piano; at times, the music evokes the atmosphere of chamber music, at others, Eastern and jazz styles reminiscent of Hiromi Uehara, or even the experimental approach of Alain Rochette (from the band Present). When the sound grows heavier, it becomes dense and dark, yet the strings and Eeva Rajakangas are always there, ensuring we never quite plunge over the precipice."Tarina" ventures into new territory; while Eeva sings and phrases with great freedom, she does so in tandem with a band that evokes the anarchic melodies of the Lounge Lizards, until the violins launch into a sort of tango reminiscent of the track "Palmiers En Pots" by the Belgian group Aksak Maboul. It is not even far-fetched to draw parallels with the Rock in Opposition scene; one can even detect traces of the early, defiant Bj�rk, alongside the bass-clarinet blues of Jaakko Arola."Vesi" evokes a violin-infused cabaret sung by Ute Lemper, yet the arrangements steer the sound toward danceable rhythms infused with punk currents, waves that surge in and recede. The band adapts perfectly to this variety of styles, skillfully navigating the challenge of maintaining overall cohesion. They stand as an impenetrable, unbreakable shield, much like the Baltic Shield, reflecting that Nordic light which lasts for months; a duration that pales in comparison to the enduring scope of their musical and artistic vision.

items.body: English post-punk band Killing Joke released their self-titled debut album, “Killing Joke,” on 5 October 1980 through E.G. Records, distributed by Polydor Records. The record turns 46 this year. Killing Joke recorded the album in August 1980 at Marquee Studios in London and produced it themselves, with Phil Harding as engineer. Drummer Paul Ferguson described the sessions as recorded live with “no overdubs to speak of.” The eight-track UK LP runs: “Requiem” “Wardance” “Tomorrow’s World” “Bloodsport” “The Wait” “Complications” “S.O.36” “Primitive” The original US pressing added “Change,” the B-side of the “Requiem” single, between “Complications” and “S.O.36.” “Wardance” came out as a single in February 1980, ahead of the album, and “Requiem” followed as a single in September 1980. The album entered the UK Albums Chart on 25 October 1980 at number 41 and later peaked at number 39. Its cover collages a photograph by Don McCullin of CS gas clashes in Derry, Northern Ireland, in 1971, designed by Mike Coles. In 2019, Pitchfork placed the album at number 9 on its list of the 33 best industrial albums of all time. “The Wait” was covered by Metallica on the 1987 “Garage Days Re-Revisited” EP and later included on “Garage Inc.,” “Primitive” was covered by Helmet in 1993, and “Requiem” was covered by Foo Fighters in 1997 as a B-side to “Everlong.” About Killing Joke Killing Joke formed in October 1978 in Notting Hill, London. Jaz Coleman (vocals, keyboards) and Paul Ferguson (drums) met in late 1978 and placed an announcement in Melody Maker in February 1979 reading “Bass, lead, to tell the killing joke, we mean it man!” Guitarist Geordie Walker and bassist Martin “Youth” Glover answered and completed the original line-up. The band released its debut EP, “Turn to Red,” as a 10-inch on 26 October 1979 on Malicious Damage, the label Killing Joke ran with graphic artist Mike Coles. Recorded in August 1979 at Gooseberry Sound in London, the EP drew airplay from BBC Radio 1’s John Peel. The “Almost Red” EP followed that November, and the single “Nervous System,” with “Turn to Red” as its B-side, came out in December 1979. Killing Joke then signed to E.G. Records for the self-titled debut album, released on 5 October 1980. The band’s next albums were “What’s THIS For…!” (1981) and “Revelations” (1982), after which Youth left the band and was replaced by Paul Raven on bass. “Fire Dances” followed in 1983 and “Night Time” in 1985, the album that carried the single “Love Like Blood” and brought the band its widest chart exposure to date. Killing Joke continued recording and touring into the 2010s with albums including “Absolute Dissent” (2010), “MMXII” (2012) and “Pylon” (2015), with Jaz Coleman and Geordie Walker as the group’s only constant members. Geordie Walker died in November 2023 at the age of 64, as Side-Line reported at the time. The band’s 1980 debut album remains the record that introduced the Killing Joke sound now marking its 46th anniversary this October.

items.body: Colossloth released a video for “Encoded Divinity” on 3 October 2026, a track from the album “The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites.” The album came out 2 October 2026 on Cold Spring Records, the project’s sixth release for the label. The video was produced by HAONDOKU Productions. The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites by Colossloth Watch the video for ‘Encoded Divinity’ The video is available on YouTube: COLOSSLOTH – ‘Encoded Divinity’ Promo Video. “Encoded Divinity” opens the album and runs 5:08. ‘The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites’ tracklist The album was announced in September with its full tracklist: “Encoded Divinity” (5:08) “Calculate Your Revolution” (7:00) “Awaiting MENA” (9:04) “Undertow Atlas” (10:34) “Only Adrift” (8:00) Cold Spring describes the album as centered on Theta Noir, a collective built around worship of Mena, a fictional artificial intelligence deity. The label calls the record “an automaton chant of cybernetic worship.” The album is available on CD in a matt-laminate digipak (catalogue number CSR375CD) through Cold Spring’s webstore, and for download via Bandcamp. Colossloth played an album launch show at The Globe in Glossop on 3 October 2026, alongside T.A.G.C. (Adi Newton of Clock DVA), Satøri and Llyn Y Cwn. Further dates follow on 7 November at St Anne’s in Barnstaple with Satøri and A Waste of Damnation, and from 27 to 29 November at Sheffield General Cemetery’s In The Black Midwinter event with The Golden Age of Doing Nothing and Decommissioned Forests. About Colossloth Colossloth is the solo project of Leicester, UK musician Wooly Woolaston, active since 2008. Woolaston has described Colossloth as “a one man Experimental Electronic artist where there are no rules to recording or playing music,” with a sound that has moved from long guitar drones toward harsher electronics with sections of melody. Woolaston released Colossloth’s first album through Doom Structure in 2008, followed by releases on Doom Mantra Records in 2009 and Dark Meadow Recordings in 2011. He later signed to Cold Spring Records, releasing “Anchored By Lungs” (2014), “Outstretch Your Hand for the Impress of Truth” (2015), “Heathen Needles” (2017), “Plague Alone” (2020) and “Promethean Meat” (2022), the latter incorporating drum samples and harsher rhythmic elements. Colossloth also appeared on the label’s “Arise – A Cold Spring Sampler” compilation alongside Coil, Merzbow and Mz.412, among others. Colossloth’s fifth Cold Spring album, “The Harmony Knife,” followed on 28 February 2025, a concept record drawing on Ted Kaczynski’s “Industrial Society and Its Future” and its argument for the psychological necessity of struggle, known as “the power process.” “The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites,” released 2 October 2026, is Colossloth’s sixth album for Cold Spring Records, now accompanied by a video for its opening track, “Encoded Divinity.”

items.body: Swedish duo Svaj. released a remix of the alan is waiting track “where you disappear” on 2 October 2026. The one-track single, titled “where you disappear (Svaj. Rebuild),” streams on Spotify and is available for download on Bandcamp and Subvert. The original song was written and sung by alan is waiting, the recording name of a Stockholm-based electronic artist whose debut album, “The Last of You,” came out in 2024. Svaj., the duo of Anders O Öhgren and Tomas Z Westberg based in Blackeberg, Stockholm, reworked the track for the remix. The release keeps alan is waiting’s original vocals. In a newsletter announcement, Svaj. described the result as “a wonky, New Order-tinged full-on synth-pop hit song.” where you disappear – Svaj. rebuild by Svaj., alan is waiting A visualizer for “where you disappear (Svaj. Rebuild)” is available on YouTube. About Svaj. Svaj. is the Stockholm duo of Anders O Öhgren and Tomas Z Westberg, based in the Blackeberg district of the city. The duo releases through its own TZW Produktion imprint. Svaj.’s Bandcamp profile describes its sound as “voice, electronics and bass. Minimal, experimental and industrial, yet melodic and danceable,” and compares it to Joy Division and Front 242. Svaj. issued its debut EP, “Rewind,” in March 2022. The songs reworked tracks originally recorded on tape in 1988, revisited with a Yamaha CS-10 synthesizer and a 1960s Tandberg reel-to-reel recorder. The duo’s second release, “Until We Fall,” followed in 2023. In 2024, Svaj. released the single “Cut Me Up,” a reworking of a song first written by Alien Waveform in 1989 and later issued as “Contagion” on the 1993 compilation “Tapping the Wires (A Selection of Futuristic Electro Mindbeats).” The digital single included a remix by UK industrial act Portion Control. The same year, Svaj. contributed “Brända Barn,” a reworking of a 1980 Swedish punk song, to the six-act compilation “SVÄRTA.” Svaj. released its third collection, “Maggots,” a six-track release, on 17 May 2025 through TZW Produktion on vinyl, CD and digital formats. The record includes a cover of John Cale’s 1974 track “Fear Is a Man’s Best Friend” and features contributions from Perra Wikström on contrabass and guitar and vocal effects from Devoid. Svaj. issued four music videos from “Maggots” through 2025, for “Experience,” “Fear,” “Portent” and, in October 2025, “Piglet.” The duo released the single “Patterns” on 19 February 2026. Svaj.’s catalog now runs from the 2022 “Rewind” EP through this month’s “where you disappear (Svaj. Rebuild)” remix.
